Reduced Density Matrices Through Machine Learning

Awwab A. Azam Thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Florida, Gainesville, USA    Lexu Zhao Thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida 32611, USA    Jiabin Yu Email: yujiabin@ufl.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida 32611, USA Affiliation: Quantum Theory Project, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
Abstract

nn-particle reduced density matrices (nn-RDMs) play a central role in understanding correlated phases of matter, but their calculation is often computationally inefficient for strongly-correlated states at large system sizes. In this work, we use neural network (NN) architectures to accelerate and even predict nn-RDMs for large systems. Our underlying intuition is that, for gapped states, nn-RDMs are often smooth functions over the Brillouin zone (BZ) and are therefore interpolable, allowing NNs trained on small-size systems to predict large-size ones. Building on this, we devise two NNs: (i) a self-attention NN that maps random RDMs to physical ones, and (ii) a Sinusoidal Representation Network (SIREN) that directly maps momentum-space coordinates to RDM values. We test the NNs on RDMs in three 2D models: the pair-pair correlation functions of the Richardson model of superconductivity, the translationally-invariant Hartree-Fock (HF) 1-RDM in a four-band repulsive model, and the translation-breaking HF 1-RDM in the half-filled Hubbard model. We find that a SIREN trained on a 6×66\times 6 momentum mesh and a SIREN trained on 44 tilted meshes (each of which has 1212 momentum points) can predict the 18×1818\times 18 pair-pair correlation function with a relative accuracy of 94.29%94.29\% and 93.77%93.77\%, respectively. NNs trained on 6×66\times 6 and 8×88\times 8 meshes provide high-quality initial guesses for 50×5050\times 50 translation-invariant HF and 30×3030\times 30 fully translation-breaking-allowed HF, reducing the required number of iterations by up to 91.63%91.63\% and 92.78%92.78\%, respectively, compared to random initializations. Our results illustrate the potential of NN-based methods for interpolable nn-RDMs, which might open a new avenue for future research on strongly correlated phases.

Introduction Understanding strongly correlated phases of matter is a central topic in condensed matter physics. The rapid progress of neural-network (NN) methods has created new opportunities for studying strongly correlated quantum phases via NN-based wavefunction ansatzes  [11, 105, 37, 82, 19, 59, 51, 108, 128, 50, 58, 76, 81, 70, 1, 119, 123, 116, 106, 71, 77, 45, 139, 84, 15, 88, 12, 141, 113, 120, 73, 83, 62, 140, 135, 107, 111, 40, 80, 16, 17, 75, 117, 33, 85, 44, 14, 67, 31, 118, 68], which have been applied to various systems including Hubbard model  [105, 20, 82, 56, 18, 59, 118]. One notable type of such NN ansatze uses the self-attention mechanism [137] to construct correlated orbitals from single-particle orbitals, expressing the many-body wavefunction as a linear combination of a small number of Slater determinants formed from these correlated orbitals  [108, 140, 135, 33, 86]. In this work, we propose a different way of using machine learning (or NNs) to understand strongly-correlated states—by focusing on their reduced density matrices.

Given a many-body Hamiltonian, the zero-temperature nn-particle reduced density matrix (nn-RDM) is defined as

O𝒌1​α1,𝒌2​α2,…,𝒌n​αn,𝒌1′​α1′,𝒌2′​α2′,…,𝒌n′​αn′=⟨c𝒌1​α1†​c𝒌2​α2†​…​c𝒌n​αn†​c𝒌1′​α1′​c𝒌2′​α2′​…​c𝒌n′​αn′⟩,\displaystyle\begin{split}&O_{\bm{k}_{1}\alpha_{1},\bm{k}_{2}\alpha_{2},...,\bm{k}_{n}\alpha_{n},\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}\alpha_{1}^{\prime},\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}\alpha_{2}^{\prime},...,\bm{k}_{n}^{\prime}\alpha_{n}^{\prime}}\\ &\quad=\left\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}_{1}\alpha_{1}}c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}_{2}\alpha_{2}}...c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}_{n}\alpha_{n}}c_{\bm{k}_{1}^{\prime}\alpha_{1}^{\prime}}c_{\bm{k}_{2}^{\prime}\alpha_{2}^{\prime}}...c_{\bm{k}_{n}^{\prime}\alpha_{n}^{\prime}}\right\rangle\ ,\end{split} (1)

where ⟨…⟩\langle...\rangle represents the average with respect to the ground state(s), and c𝒌​α†c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\alpha} creates a particle with Bloch momentum 𝒌\bm{k} and intra-unit-cell degree of freedom α\alpha (which labels sub-lattice, orbital, spin, etc).

The nn-RDM plays a vital role in understanding strongly correlated states [22, 66, 28, 21, 142, 34, 93, 35, 94, 126, 130, 97, 138, 96, 125, 121, 5, 48, 13, 124, 72, 65, 25]. First, the Hamiltonians of realistic condensed matter systems almost always involve only one-body and two-body terms, implying that the 1-RDM and 2-RDM are sufficient to evaluate the many-body ground-state energy [22, 32, 89, 90, 10, 98, 57]. This observation lies at the heart of semidefinite programming approaches [136, 104, 142, 91, 92, 93, 27, 95, 99, 100, 122], which iteratively compute the 2-RDM. Second, the order parameters that characterize spontaneous symmetry breaking—such as charge-density waves and magnetism—often depend only on the 1-RDM [36], which explains the effectiveness of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method [134].

Given the importance of the nn-RDMs, it would be transformative to design an NN that predicts nn-RDMs for a given Hamiltonian, particularly for large systems where existing algorithms become computationally inefficient. Because semidefinite programming and the HF algorithm compute nn-RDMs iteratively, the NN predictions (even if they are not exactly precise) can serve as an initial guess which is already very close to the converged state, thereby dramatically reducing the number of iterations required for convergence. Furthermore, 2-RDM methods (e.g. semidefinite programming) are inherently susceptible to converging to non-physical solutions, but comparing the converged solution to the NN predictions may help determine whether the converged solution is physical, since the NNs are trained on physical 2-RDMs and thus their predictions are likely to be physical.

In this work, we develop two such NNs: (i) a self-attention NN that maps random initial 1-RDMs to the predicted final 1-RDMs, and (ii) a Sinusoidal Representation Network (SIREN) [131] that learns nn-RDMs and interpolates them to denser 𝒌\bm{k} meshes (App. A). The underlying reason for the existence of such NNs lies in the interpolable nature of nn-RDMs. These NNs are trained on small system sizes, where the nn-RDMs can be efficiently computed using existing methods, and are then used to predict the nn-RDMs of much larger systems. We first benchmark SIREN on the pair-pair correlation functions of the superconducting ground states of the exactly-solvable Richardson model, and find that a SIREN trained only on the 6×66\times 6 mesh can achieve a relative accuracy of 94.29%94.29\% for predictions on 18×1818\times 18. Additionally, a SIREN trained on four tilted meshes, each of which has 1212 𝒌\bm{k} points, achieves a relative accuracy of 93.77%93.77\% on 18×1818\times 18 (App. B).

We then benchmark the self-attention NN on the translationally-invariant HF calculations for a four-band model with short-range repulsion. Our results show that an NN trained only on 6×66\times 6 and 8×88\times 8 meshes can maintain a relatively low mean squared error (MSE, below 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}) for up to 50×5050\times 50. Furthermore, for momentum mesh sizes from 10×10,12×12,…,50×5010\times 10,12\times 12,\dots,50\times 50, using the NN predictions as the initial 1-RDM for HF calculations results in a 91.61%91.61\%—94.24%94.24\% reduction in the number of HF iterations required for convergence compared to the HF calculations with random initialization (App. C).

We finally benchmark both NNs on the HF calculations that allow translation breaking in half-filled Hubbard model. We again compare the HF iteration numbers between using the NN-predicted final 1-RDM as initial 1-RDMs and using the random initial 1-RDMs. We find a significant (60.79%60.79\%—92.78%92.78\%) reduction in the number of HF iterations for up to 30×3030\times 30 using SIRENs trained only on the 8×88\times 8 mesh, and a self-attention NN trained only on 8×88\times 8 and 10×1010\times 10 meshes (App. D). The remarkable reduction in iteration numbers for HF calculations—that forbid or allow translational breaking—demonstrates the potential of NNs for speeding up the calculation of or even the precise prediction of RDMs of large-size systems.

We note that our work is the first to construct NNs that predict large-size nn-RDMs for strongly correlated phases, exploiting the interpolable structure of nn-RDMs in momentum space. In contrast to our work, previous developments of NNs that involve RDMs either focus on real-space 1-RDM in ab initio calculations (such as density functional theory) to establish maps between 11-RDM and other quantities [127, 87, 46, 71, 41] or 2-RDM for chemical molecules [7, 24]. Our general idea of using NNs for interpolable nn-RDMs, exemplified by our implementations for pair–pair correlation functions and 1-RDMs, might open a new avenue for studying strongly correlated states.

Interpolability of nn-RDM In this section, we discuss the interpolability of the nn-RDM in the BZ. As shown in Eq. 1, the nn-RDM is a function of 2​n2n Bloch momenta; for a finite 2D system with L×LL\times L unit cells and periodic boundary conditions these momenta lie on an L×LL\times L mesh in the BZ, and increasing the system size to a commensurate L′L^{\prime} simply inserts additional momentum points between those of the original mesh (Fig. 1) while the Bloch momenta always occupy the same convex hull—the BZ.

If nn-RDM is a smooth function of 2​n2n Bloch momenta in the thermodynamic limit, then its values on extra momentum points can be interpolated from those on the original L×LL\times L grid. Namely, although the nn-RDMs are extrapolated from small to large real-space system sizes, they are in fact interpolated in momentum space. This smoothness condition is naturally satisfied for gapped ground states, and even for gapless states certain combinations of nn-RDMs (e.g., the pair–pair correlator in the Richardson model  [115, 114, 26]) can remain smooth functions of the Bloch momenta. Thus, smooth nn-RDMs (or smooth combinations thereof) are ubiquitous in condensed-matter systems.

These properties are crucial for NNs to function effectively. Our goal is to train a NN on small system sizes and use it to predict nn-RDMs for large systems. As large size RDM always lie within the fixed convex hull of the training distribution, predicting smooth nn-RDMs for large systems from the training data on small systems is an interpolation (as opposed to extrapolation) task. Furthermore, smooth nn-RDMs are continuous functions, so they can be well approximated by NNs (in principle with an arbitrary degree of precision [23, 53, 109], given no restrictions on the number of parameters). Therefore, our task here is analogous to image-resolution enhancement, where extra pixel points are inserted to enhance the resolution—a problem where NNs already perform well [63], implying the feasibility of our approach.

NN Architectures We now discuss the NN architectures used in this work. We will focus on the 1-RDM (O𝒌​α,𝒌′​α′=⟨c𝒌​α†​c𝒌′​α′⟩,O_{\bm{k}\alpha,\bm{k}^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime}}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\alpha}c_{\bm{k}^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime}}\rangle\ , with α=1,2,…,ξ\alpha=1,2,...,\xi) in momentum space and discuss the generalization at the end. Particularly, we focus on fixed momentum transfer 𝒌−𝒌′=𝒒\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}=\bm{q}, where 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 means translation-invariance and we will include more than one 𝒒\bm{q} for spontaneous translation-symmetry breaking cases.

The two NNs described in this section can be trained on small-size O𝒒O^{\bm{q}} (generated via HF calculations) to predict large-size O𝒒O^{\bm{q}}. We will only outline the key steps here, and leave details to App. A.

The first NN architecture that we construct is a self-attention NN (Fig. 2) that maps a random initial 1-RDM Oinit𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{init}} to a predicted final 1-RDM Oout𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{out}}. It is trained on small L×LL\times L using numerically generated pairs {Oinit𝒒​(𝒌)},{Otgt𝒒​(𝒌)}\{O^{\bm{q}}_{\mathrm{init}}(\bm{k})\},\{O^{\bm{q}}_{\mathrm{tgt}}(\bm{k})\}, where LL denotes the number of lattice sites along each side, and Otgt𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{tgt}} denotes the true final 1-RDM from the HF calculation. The overall structure is shown in Fig. 2(a). We first preprocess the 1-RDM O𝒌,α​α′𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}} into a set of standardized [42, 69] 2​ξ22\xi^{2}-dimensional real vectors 𝒙~i\tilde{\bm{x}}_{i} at the ithi^{\text{th}} Bloch momentum, which is then fed into the self-attention NN consisting of NN attention layers. All the 𝒙~i\tilde{\bm{x}}_{i} are linearly transformed and stacked into the input matrix H(0)H^{(0)} of size L2×DL^{2}\times D for the first attention layer. Subsequently, the ℓth\ell^{\text{th}} attention layer maps H(ℓ−1)↦H(ℓ)H^{(\ell-1)}\mapsto H^{(\ell)} with l=1,2,..,Nl=1,2,..,N, after which H(N)H^{(N)} is decoded back to Oout𝒒​(𝒌)O_{\mathrm{out}}^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}), which is the predicted final 1–RDM. Within the ℓth{\ell}^{\text{th}} attention layer (Fig. 2(b)), we have an attention block, a feedforward network (FFN), Dropout, and LayerNorm, where the last two (Dropout and LayerNorm) are common NN layers to prevent overfitting and improve optimization stability [133, 2]. Each attention block uses NheadN_{\text{head}} parallel heads (Fig. 2(c)); in head hh, the per-head width is dk≡D/Nheadd_{k}\equiv D/N_{\text{head}}. We form α(h)=H(ℓ−1)​Wα(h)\alpha^{(h)}=H^{(\ell-1)}W_{\alpha}^{(h)}, where α∈{Q,K,V}\alpha\in\{Q,K,V\} for the “query”, “key”, and “value” matrices respectively, and each Wα(h)∈ℝD×dkW_{\alpha}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{k}} is learnable.

Our construction modifies the original self-attention mechanism [137] in two major ways. First, to encode the momentum information, we introduce a novel positional encoding scheme that uses a learnable bias Bi​jB_{ij} to increase or decrease the attention scores based on the momentum-space separation between 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i} and 𝒌j\bm{k}_{j} (Fig. 2(d)). Second, we also use a learnable scalar ss [103] to avoid “attention fading” and better enable the NN to handle variable-size inputs.

The second NN architecture we use is SIREN [131], which represents the 1–RDM as a set of smooth, periodic functions of 𝒌\bm{k} coordinates, thereby enabling interpolation to denser 𝒌\bm{k} meshes. The overall structure is shown in Fig. 3(a). We first map BZ 𝒌\bm{k} points to normalized coordinates 𝒗⁡(𝒌)∈[−1,1]2\bm{v}(\bm{k})\in[-1,1]^{2}. Then, for each fixed (α,α′)(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}), the real and imaginary parts of O𝒌,α​α′𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}} are a function of 𝒗\bm{v}, and we train a scalar function Φθ\Phi_{\theta} such that Φθ​(𝒗)≈Re[Oα​α′𝒒​(𝒌)]\Phi_{\theta}(\bm{v})\approx\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[O^{\bm{q}}_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}(\bm{k})] or Im[Oα​α′𝒒​(𝒌)]\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}[O^{\bm{q}}_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}(\bm{k})]\ . Specifically, we construct each Φθ\Phi_{\theta} using 4 hidden layers of sinusoidal functions followed by a linear function, and finally assemble Φθ\Phi_{\theta} for different (α,α′)(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}) to give the final predicted O𝒒​(𝒌𝒊)O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k_{i}}). To train the SIREN on a L1×L1L_{1}\times L_{1} mesh, we introduce a custom loss function with three parts (Fig. 3(b)): (i) the mean-squared error (MSE) on the smaller system of size L1L_{1}, (ii) a novel consistency term that evaluates Φθ\Phi_{\theta} on a denser mesh of size L2L_{2}, averages over a chosen symmetry subgroup GG, downsamples back to size L1L_{1}, and then computes the MSE with the true final L1×L1L_{1}\times L_{1} 1-RDM, and (iii) a statistical prior consisting of TV/Hessian regularization at a randomly sampled set of points [131]. It is straightforward to generalize our NN architectures to any special combination of nn-RDM (with n>1n>1) that only depends on one Bloch momentum (with other momenta fixed just like O𝒌,α​α′𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}). Beyond one-momentum quantities, the SIREN can be applied to the pair-pair correlation function (a special 22-RDM) for superconductors, which depends on two momenta, as we show in the subsequent section. In general, we expect the SIREN can naturally be extended to quantities that are a smooth function of more than two momenta.

Pair-Pair Correlation Functions In this section, we benchmark the SIREN on the pair-pairing correlation function for superconductivity. As a benchmark, we consider the exactly-solvable Richardson model  [115, 114, 26] in 2 dimensions on an L×LL\times L 𝒌\bm{k} mesh

H=∑𝒌,sε𝒌​c𝒌​s†​c𝒌​s+uL2​∑𝒌A𝒌†​∑𝒌′A𝒌′,H=\sum_{\bm{k},s}\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}\,c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}s}c_{\bm{k}s}+\frac{u}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{k}}A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\sum_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\ , (2)

where L2L^{2} is the number of lattice sites, ε𝒌=t⁡(cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky)\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}=t(\cos k_{x}+\cos k_{y}) with t=0.1t=0.1, u=−1u=-1, and c𝒌​s†c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}s} creates an electron with Bloch momentum 𝒌\bm{k} and spin ss. We work in the number-conserving case, where the pair–pair correlation function is just the Cooper–channel matrix channel of 2-RDM C𝒌​𝒌′=O𝒌↑,−𝒌↓,𝒌′↑,−𝒌′↓=⟨A𝒌†A𝒌′⟩C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}=O_{\bm{k}\uparrow,-\bm{k}\downarrow,\bm{k}^{\prime}\uparrow,-\bm{k}^{\prime}\downarrow}=\big\langle A^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\,A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\big\rangle, as ⟨A𝒌⟩=⟨c𝒌↑†​c−𝒌↓†⟩=0\langle A_{\bm{k}}\rangle=\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\uparrow}\,c^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}\downarrow}\rangle=0. The model is exactly solved for electron filling 1/61/6 for L=6L=6, L=12L=12, and L=18L=18 (see details in App. B). We then trained a SIREN on the obtained C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} for L=6L=6, and tested the precision of the prediction on larger sizes up to L=18L=18 by evaluating the relative accuracy rn=(1−MSEmax​(C)−min​(C))r_{n}=\left(1-\frac{\sqrt{\text{MSE}}}{\text{max}(C)-\text{min}(C)}\right). (Here “MSE” stands for the mean squared error between the NN-predicted final and the true final correlation function, as discussed in App. B.)

Remarkably, the SIREN trained only on L=6L=6 can predict C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} for a larger size (L=18L=18) with a rather high accuracy of rn=94.29%r_{n}=94.29\% (see Fig. 4 for comparison), verifying the validity of our method.

To further demonstrate the efficiency of our method, we consider smaller training meshes. Because the dimension of the Hilbert space scales exponentially with system size, it is often computationally much cheaper to calculate RDMs for several smaller momentum meshes rather than for a single larger mesh. Building on this insight, we trained an additional SIREN on C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} for 4 tilted meshes (see App. B), each of which has 1212 𝒌\bm{k} points, as depicted in Fig. 5. The trained SIREN is then able to predict C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} for the 18×1818\times 18 mesh with a relative accuracy of 93.77%93.77\%, which further underscores the efficiency of our method.

Translationally-Invariant HF We further benchmark our self-attention NN on translationally-invariant HF for the 1-RDM. The final true 1-RDM is calculated via the HF algorithm starting from a random initial 1-RDM. The model we consider is a L×LL\times L square lattice with a four-component spinor per unit cell, short-range hopping terms, and repulsive interaction.

We choose the hopping such that the lower two single-particle bands have a nontrivial time-reversal–invariant Z2{Z}_{2} topology [60]. We perform the translationally-invariant HF calculations at filling ν=1\nu=1 for L=6,8,10,12,…​50L=6,8,10,12,\dots 50. Using this data, we train a self-attention NN on 10,00010,000 (initial 1-RDM, true final 1-RDM) pairs for each of L=6,8L=6,8 (see App. C). In order to evaluate its effectiveness, we feed 1,0001,000 random initial 1-RDMs for each of L=10,12,…​50L=10,12,\dots 50 into the trained NN to obtain the corresponding predicted final 1-RDMs. We then use those predicted final 1-RDMs as initial conditions for the HF calculation and record the number of iterations to converge, and compare it with HF started from a random initialization. Particularly, we find that it takes an average of 8.0578.057 iteration steps to converge when using the predicted final 1-RDMs for L=50L=50 as the initial 1-RDMs for HF, as compared to an average of 96.30196.301 iterations with random initial 1-RDMs. Thus, our NN, when trained on L=6,8L=6,8, results in a 91.6391.63% reduction in the number of iterations required for HF convergence for L=50L=50. The percent reduction for other system sizes is shown in Fig. 6. Notably, they are all above 90%90\%. (see App. C for details).

HF Allowing Translational Breaking Finally, we benchmark both NNs for HF calculations that allow any kind of translation breaking that is compatible with the momentum meshes. We focus on the Hubbard model on a 2D square lattice [54, 55] with onsite UU and hopping t=1t=1. We consider the half filling and assume that a spin U⁡(1)U(1) is conserved. Then, the 1-RDM that serves as the order parameters is spin-resolved: [Oσ]𝒌​𝒌′=⟨c𝒌′​σ†c𝒌​σ⟩,σ∈{↑,↓}[O_{\sigma}]_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}^{\prime}\sigma}c_{\bm{k}\sigma}\rangle,\quad\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}. We perform zero-total-spin HF calculations for L=8,10,…,20L=8,10,\dots,20 and U=1,2,3U=1,2,3, allowing all translation breaking that is compatible with the momentum mesh. The lowest-energy converged [Oσ]𝒌​𝒌′[O_{\sigma}]_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} are not zero only when 𝒌′−𝒌\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{k} is (π,π)(\pi,\pi) and (0,0)(0,0), which is consistent with the (π,π)(\pi,\pi)-antiferromagnetism at half filling [52]. We train both a self-attention NN and a SIREN. The self-attention NN was trained on L=8L=8 and L=10L=10 for U=1U=1 only (due to limited training data), and tested on L=12,…​30L=12,\dots 30. The SIRENs were trained on L=8L=8 for U=1,2,3U=1,2,3, and tested on L=10,…​30L=10,\dots 30. For evaluation, we again compute the percent reduction in the number of HF iterations using the predicted final 1-RDM as the initial guess versus using a random initial 1-RDM, and observe a dramatic reduction (73.27%CLOSE(73.27\%—OPEN92.78%)92.78\%) at larger sizes (​i.e.,L≥18{\emph{i.e.}},\,L\geq 18). Fig. 7 shows the percent reduction plotted as a function of LL for different values of UU.

Conclusion and Discussion: In summary, we showed that large-size nn-RDMs can be predicted by NNs trained on small-size nn-RDMs, with benchmarks on the pair-pair correlation function and translationally-invariant/breaking HF. One immediate future step is to use these NNs to help predict new correlated states in other systems. Certainly, the development of NNs for general 22-RDMs (or nn-RDM with n>2n>2) is an important future direction. The application of our NNs to strongly correlated systems, such as moiré materials, is also expected to yield useful results.

Supplementary Information

Appendix A NN Architecture

We train NNs on nn-RDMs computed on small L×LL\times L lattices and use them to predict nn-RDMs for larger systems, exploiting their smooth, periodic structure over the BZ. We use two complementary architectures: (i) a self-attention NN that treats momenta as tokens and learns n-RDMs via self–attention [137, 3, 129], and (ii) an implicit neural representation (INR) in the style of NeRF/SIREN that models n-RDMs as a continuous periodic function evaluable at arbitrary system sizes [101, 131].

A.1 Self-Attention NN Architecture for the 1-RDM

We start with the self-attention NN for 1-RDM.

A.1.1 physical set-up

The self-attention NN is applied on a 1-RDM in two spatial dimensions (2D) for the examples in App. C and App. D. Therefore, in this part, we will first discuss 1-RDM that will be fed into the NN. The 1-RDM has the general form

O𝒌​α,𝒌′​α′=⟨c𝒌​α†​c𝒌′​α′⟩O_{\bm{k}\alpha,\,\bm{k}^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime}}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\alpha}c_{\bm{k}^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime}}\rangle\, (3)

where 𝒌\bm{k} and 𝒌′\bm{k}^{\prime} ranges over the first BZ, α\alpha represents intra-unit-cell degrees of freedom (sublattice, orbital, spin, etc.), taking ξ\xi different values of them per 𝒌\bm{k}. c𝒌​α†c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\alpha} is the creation operator for a state with Bloch momentum 𝒌\bm{k} and index α\alpha, and ⟨…⟩\left\langle...\right\rangle is the ground state average. 𝒌\bm{k} takes L×LL\times L different values:

𝒌=(l1/L)​𝒃1+(l2/L)​𝒃2,\bm{k}=(l_{1}/L)\bm{b}_{1}+(l_{2}/L)\bm{b}_{2}\ , (4)

where l1,l2=0,1,2,…,L−1l_{1},l_{2}=0,1,2,...,L-1, and 𝒃1\bm{b}_{1} and 𝒃2\bm{b}_{2} are two primitive reciprocal lattice vectors. When the translation symmetry is not spontaneously broken, the 1-RDM is reduced to

O𝒌,α​α′=⟨c𝒌​α†​c𝒌​α′⟩,O𝒌∈ℂξ×ξ,O_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\alpha}c_{\bm{k}\alpha^{\prime}}\rangle,\quad O_{\bm{k}}\in\mathbb{C}^{\xi\times\xi}, (5)

so the tensor has shape L×L×ξ×ξL\times L\times\xi\times\xi. This is the case for App. C. When the translation symmetry is spontaneously broken, we will look at O𝒌​α,𝒌′​α′O_{\bm{k}\alpha,\bm{k}^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime}} with fixed 𝒒≡𝒌′−𝒌\bm{q}\equiv\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{k}, i.e.,

O𝒌,α​α′𝒒=O𝒌​α,𝒌+𝒒​α′.O_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}^{\bm{q}}=O_{\bm{k}\alpha,\bm{k}+\bm{q}\alpha^{\prime}}\ . (6)

For a fixed 𝒒\bm{q}, O𝒒O^{\bm{q}} is also a tensor of dimension L×L×ξ×ξL\times L\times\xi\times\xi. In the notation of O𝒌,α​α′𝒒O_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}^{\bm{q}}, the translational invariant case is just to focus on O𝒌,α​α′𝒒=0O_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}^{\bm{q}=0}. Therefore, regardless of the translation symmetry, O𝒌,α​α′𝒒O_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}^{\bm{q}} has dimension L×L×ξ×ξL\times L\times\xi\times\xi.

A.1.2 Preprocessing (transform 1-RDM to NN input)

With the 1-RDM O𝒒O^{\bm{q}} defined above, we now show how they are transformed into fixed-length vectors and standardized to form the input for our self-attention NN, which is preprocessing part of Fig. 2(a). From Eq. 4, the BZ grid has L×LL\times L momenta with the iith momentum labelled as 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i} (i=1,2,…,L2i=1,2,...,L^{2}).

For each 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i}, we consider the corresponding 1-RDM block, O𝒒​(𝒌i)O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}_{i}). We transform (flatten) this matrix into a real vector 𝒙⁡(𝒌i)∈ℝ 2​ξ2\bm{x}(\bm{k}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{\,2\xi^{2}} in the following way. For the translation-invariant case, O𝒒​(𝒌i)∈ℂξ×ξO^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}_{i})\in\mathbb{C}^{\xi\times\xi} and 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 (App. C),

𝒙⁡(𝒌i)≡[v​e​c​(Re⁡O𝒒​(𝒌i))v​e​c​(Im⁡O𝒒​(𝒌i))]∈ℝ 2​ξ2.\bm{x}(\bm{k}_{i})\equiv\begin{bmatrix}vec\big(\operatorname{Re}O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}_{i})\big)\\ vec\big(\operatorname{Im}O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}_{i})\big)\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{\,2\xi^{2}}. (7)

Here the operation vec(…) simply turns a matrix into a long column vector by transposing and then stacking its rows from top to bottom. Namely,

[v​e​c​(M)](α−1)​ξ+α′≡Mα​α′,α,α′=1,…,ξ.\big[vec(M)\big]_{(\alpha-1)\xi+\alpha^{\prime}}\equiv M_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}},\qquad\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}=1,\ldots,\xi. (8)

For the specific translational-symmetry-breaking case in Hubbard model discussed in App. D, we have O𝒒​(𝒌i)O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}_{i}) real. Furthermore, 𝒒\bm{q} only takes two values , 𝒒∈{0,𝑸}\bm{q}\in\{0,\bm{Q}\} with 𝑸=(π,π)\bm{Q}=(\pi,\pi). Thus, in this case, we do not split the 1-RDM into real/imaginary parts; instead we stack the two qq-blocks:

𝒙⁡(𝒌i)≡[v​e​c​(O0​(𝒌i))v​e​c​(O𝑸​(𝒌i))]∈ℝ 2​ξ2.\bm{x}(\bm{k}_{i})\equiv\begin{bmatrix}vec\big(O^{0}(\bm{k}_{i})\big)\\ vec\big(O^{\bm{Q}}(\bm{k}_{i})\big)\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{\,2\xi^{2}}. (9)

Therefore, both cases (Eqs. 7 and 9) leads to 𝒙⁡(𝒌i)\bm{x}(\bm{k}_{i}) with the same shape, thus the components of 𝒙⁡(𝒌i)\bm{x}(\bm{k}_{i}) can be labeled by f∈{1,…,2​ξ2}f\in\{1,\dots,2\xi^{2}\}. See App. C and App. D for more details about the preprocessing steps for each model. For one BZ mesh, stack the L2L^{2} vectors 𝒙⁡(𝒌i)\bm{x}(\bm{k}_{i}) row-wise to form

X≡[𝒙​(𝒌1)⊤𝒙​(𝒌L2)⊤]∈ℝL2×2​ξ2.X\equiv\begin{bmatrix}\bm{x}(\bm{k}_{1})^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \bm{x}(\bm{k}_{L^{2}})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times 2\xi^{2}}. (10)

A single training sample consists of two 1-RDMs over the entire BZ, an initial Oinit𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{init}} and a final (target) Otgt𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{tgt}}. Here, “init\mathrm{init}” means the 1-RDM we used to start HF; “tgt\mathrm{tgt}” means the true final 1-RDM we obtained at zero temperature after self-consistent HF convergence. After flattening in Eqs. 7 and 9, they become:

X(β)≡[𝒙(β)​(𝒌1)⊤𝒙(β)​(𝒌L2)⊤]∈ℝL2×2​ξ2,β∈{init,tgt}.X^{(\beta)}\equiv\begin{bmatrix}\bm{x}^{(\beta)}(\bm{k}_{1})^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \bm{x}^{(\beta)}(\bm{k}_{L^{2}})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{\,L^{2}\times 2\xi^{2}},\qquad\beta\in\{\mathrm{init},\mathrm{tgt}\}. (11)

Define means and standard deviations over all 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i} and all NsampleN_{\text{sample}} training samples with β∈{init,tgt}\beta\in\{\text{init},\text{tgt}\} , for each feature f∈{1,…,2​ξ2}f\in\{1,\dots,2\xi^{2}\}:

μf(β)≡1Nsample​L2​∑sample∑i=1L2Xi,f(β),(σf(β))2≡1Nsample​L2−1​∑sample∑i=1L2(Xi,f(β)−μf(β))2.\mu_{f}^{(\beta)}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sample}}L^{2}}\sum_{\text{sample}}\sum_{i=1}^{L^{2}}X_{i,f}^{(\beta)},\qquad\left(\sigma_{f}^{(\beta)}\right)^{2}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sample}}L^{2}-1}\sum_{\text{sample}}\sum_{i=1}^{L^{2}}\left(X_{i,f}^{(\beta)}-\mu_{f}^{(\beta)}\right)^{2}. (12)

Note that for the translation-invariant case (App. C), we calculate the mean and standard deviation across all features (see Eq. 220). We then standardize Xinit,XtgtX_{\mathrm{init}},X_{\mathrm{tgt}} (computing the zz-score):

X~i,f(init)≡Xi,f(init)−μf(init)σf(init),X~i,f(tgt)≡Xi,f(tgt)−μf(tgt)σf(tgt),\widetilde{X}^{\mathrm{(init)}}_{i,f}\equiv\frac{X^{\mathrm{(init)}}_{i,f}-\mu^{\mathrm{(init)}}_{f}}{\sigma^{\mathrm{(init)}}_{f}},\qquad\widetilde{X}^{\mathrm{(tgt)}}_{i,f}\equiv\frac{X^{\mathrm{(tgt)}}_{i,f}-\mu^{\mathrm{(tgt)}}_{f}}{\sigma^{\mathrm{(tgt)}}_{f}}, (13)

Equivalently, for each 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i}

𝒙~(β)​(𝒌i)≡(X~i,1(β),…,X~i,2​ξ2(β))⊤∈ℝ2​ξ2.\tilde{\bm{x}}^{(\beta)}(\bm{k}_{i})\equiv\big(\widetilde{X}^{(\beta)}_{i,1},\ldots,\widetilde{X}^{(\beta)}_{i,2\xi^{2}}\big)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\xi^{2}}. (14)

In what follows, the NN input is the standardized 𝒙~(init)​(𝒌i)\tilde{\bm{x}}^{\mathrm{(init)}}(\bm{k}_{i}); for brevity we write 𝒙~i≡𝒙~(init)​(𝒌i)\tilde{\bm{x}}_{i}\equiv\tilde{\bm{x}}^{\mathrm{(init)}}(\bm{k}_{i}) unless stated otherwise. Standardization ensures that both the input and output data in the training dataset have a mean of 00 and a standard deviation of 11, which improves numerical conditioning and speeds training [42, 69]. This combined set of transformations (flattening in Eq. 7 and standardization in Eq. 13) is denoted in the preprocessing part of Fig. 2. Note that since these transformations are invertible, we can easily reverse the process to recover the predicted final 1-RDMs from the NN outputs. The matrices X~(init)\widetilde{X}^{\text{(init)}} and X~(tgt)\widetilde{X}^{\text{(tgt)}}, containing exactly the information from Oinit𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{init}} and Otgt𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{tgt}}, are thus the data we use to train the NN. During the training process, the self-attention NN parameters are optimized so that, starting from Oinit𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{init}} defined on all L2L^{2} momenta, it produces Oout𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{out}} whose values at each 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i} closely matches the Otgt𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{tgt}}. After the training, we would expect the NN to be able to make accurate predictions for Otgt𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\text{tgt}} not only for the training system size but also for larger LL.

A.1.3 Overall Structure of Attention Layers

With each local O𝒒​(𝒌i)O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}_{i}) now flattened and standardized (Eq. 7-Eq. 9) into token features 𝒙i~\tilde{\bm{x}_{i}}, we now describe the overall structure of how our model processes them through stacked attention layers to produce the predicted final 1-RDM, as shown in Fig. 2(b).

Input layer. As shown in Eqs. 7 and 9, at each momentum 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i} we have a normalized real feature vector 𝒙~i∈ℝ2​ξ2\tilde{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\xi^{2}} (flattened entries of the 1-RDM at some 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i}). We first map it to a vector of dimension DD (where DD is the “model width”):

𝒉i(0)=Win​𝒙~i+𝒃in∈ℝD,\bm{h}^{(0)}_{i}=W_{\mathrm{in}}\tilde{\bm{x}}_{i}+\bm{b}_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (15)

where Win,𝒃inW_{\text{in}},\bm{b}_{\text{in}} are learnable parameters. Stacking all 𝒉i(0)\bm{h}_{i}^{(0)} gives us a matrix H(0)H^{(0)},

H(0)=[(𝒉1(0))⊤(𝒉L2(0))⊤]∈ℝL2×D.H^{(0)}=\begin{bmatrix}(\bm{h}_{1}^{(0)})^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ (\bm{h}_{L^{2}}^{(0)})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times D}. (16)

Attention layers. We then apply NN attention layers (Fig. 2(a)) to H(0)H^{(0)} in sequence in order to produce H(N)∈ℝL2×DH^{(N)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times D}, where the ii-th row is hi(N)∈ℝDh^{(N)}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. In general, we denote the matrix H(ℓ−1)∈ℝL2×DH^{(\ell-1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times D} as the input to the ℓth\ell^{\text{th}} layer of our model, ℓ∈{1,…​N}\ell\in\{1,\dots N\}. The structure of one attention layer consists of three components: (a) one attention block discussed in Sec. A.1.4, (b) Dropout and LayerNorm discussed in Sec. A.1.5 and (c) one FFN, also discussed in Sec. A.1.5. As we will see in Sec. A.1.5, the first FFN layer (see construction in Sec. A.1.5) maps ℝD→ℝDff\mathbb{R}^{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{D_{\mathrm{ff}}} and the second maps back ℝDff→ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D_{\mathrm{ff}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{D}.

Output head. Finally, we define a linear head with which learnable parameters Wout∈ℝ2​ξ2×DW_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\xi^{2}\times D}, 𝒃out∈ℝ2​ξ2\bm{b}_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\xi^{2}} that maps each 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i} back to a vector 𝒙^i\widehat{\bm{x}}_{i}:

𝒙^i=Wout​𝒉i(N)+𝒃out.\widehat{\bm{x}}_{i}=W_{\mathrm{out}}\,\bm{h}^{(N)}_{i}+\bm{b}_{\mathrm{out}}\ . (17)

Stacking all 𝒙^i\widehat{\bm{x}}_{i} gives

X~out=[𝒙^1⊤𝒙^L2⊤]∈ℝL2×2​ξ2.\widetilde{X}_{\mathrm{out}}=\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{\bm{x}}_{1}^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \widehat{\bm{x}}_{L^{2}}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times 2\xi^{2}}. (18)

To recover the physics of 1-RDM, we de-standardize elementwise (reverse of Eq. 13):

(Xout)i,f≡(X~out)i,f​σftgt+μftgt.(X_{\mathrm{out}})_{i,f}\equiv(\widetilde{X}_{\mathrm{out}})_{i,f}\sigma^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{f}+\mu^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{f}. (19)

Note that when testing the trained NN for larger LL, we use the same μftgt\mu^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{f} and σftgt\sigma^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{f} computed from the smaller system size, since the assumption is that they possess similar distributions. We then reshape XoutX_{\mathrm{out}} to L×L×ξ×ξL\times L\times\xi\times\xi and recombine the real/imag halves to invert the flattening in Eq. 7 - Eq. 9, yielding the final predicted 1-RDM:

𝒙out(𝒌i)≡(𝒙~out(𝒌i))fσftgt+μftgt,f=1,…,2ξ2.\bm{x}_{\text{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})\equiv\bigl(\bm{\widetilde{x}}_{\mathrm{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})\bigr)_{f}\,\sigma^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{f}+\mu^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{f},\qquad f=1,\dots,2\xi^{2}. (20)
ReOout𝒒(𝒌i)≡vec−1((𝒙out(𝒌i))1:ξ2),ImOout𝒒(𝒌i)≡vec−1((𝒙out(𝒌i))ξ2+1:2​ξ2),\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}\,O^{\bm{q}}_{\mathrm{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})\equiv\operatorname{vec}^{-1}\left(\,\left(\bm{x}_{\text{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})\right)_{1:\xi^{2}}\right),\qquad\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}\,O^{\bm{q}}_{\mathrm{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})\equiv\operatorname{vec}^{-1}\left(\left(\bm{x}_{\text{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})\right)_{\xi^{2}+1:2\xi^{2}}\right), (21)
Oout𝒒​(𝒌i)=ReOout𝒒​(𝒌i)+i​ImOout𝒒​(𝒌i),O^{\bm{q}}_{\mathrm{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})=\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}O^{\bm{q}}_{\mathrm{out}}(\bm{k}_{i})+i\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}O^{\bm{q}}_{\mathrm{out}}(\bm{k}_{i}), (22)

where μf\mu_{f}, σf\sigma_{f} are defined in Eq. 12. And vec−1\operatorname{vec}^{-1} is the inverse of the vec in Eq. 7, which takes a length-ξ2\xi^{2} vector and reshapes it back into a ξ×ξ\xi\times\xi matrix using the same stacking convention from vec\mathrm{vec} (see Eq. 7). The process from Eq. 19 to Eq. 22 are shown as the decoding step in Fig. 2.

Training. For computational efficiency, we divide the training dataset into several “minibatches” (according to standard practice), where each minibatch consists of NbN_{b} (X~init,X~tgt\widetilde{X}_{\text{init}},\widetilde{X}_{\text{tgt}}) pairs. For our loss function, we use the MSE between X~out\widetilde{X}_{\text{out}} and X~tgt\widetilde{X}_{\text{tgt}} (both of which have a total of L2L^{2} elements):

ℒ=1Nb​L2​(2​ξ2)​∑b=1Nb∑i=1L2∑f=12​ξ2(X~out,i,f(b)−X~tgt,i,f(b))2.\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{N_{b}L^{2}\,(2\xi^{2})}\sum_{b=1}^{N_{b}}\sum_{i=1}^{L^{2}}\sum_{f=1}^{2\xi^{2}}\big(\widetilde{X}^{(b)}_{\text{out},i,f}-\widetilde{X}^{(b)}_{\mathrm{tgt},i,f}\big)^{2}. (23)

as indicated in Fig. 2, then take the gradient of the loss ℒ\mathcal{L} with respect to the trainable parameters (defined in Sec. A.1.5) and update the values of parameters using the AdamW optimizer [79].

A.1.4 Attention Block (multiple attention heads)

Here we describe the detailed structure of the attention block we first mentioned in Sec. A.1.3 as part of each attention layer. Each attention block includes NheadN_{\text{head}} attention heads (Fig. 2(c)). The structure of one attention head is shown in Fig. 2(d). We first introduce the Bias block in Fig. 2(d). The bias block is constructed based on the geometry-aware relative positional bias that will be used in attention heads. Intuitively speaking, attention [137] decides “which 𝒌j\bm{k}_{j} should influence 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i}.” We want this decision to respect BZ geometry and periodicity. Precisely, for each ordered pair of momenta (𝒌i,𝒌j)(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{k}_{j}) with 𝒌i=li,1L​𝒃1+li,2L​𝒃2\bm{k}_{i}=\tfrac{l_{i,1}}{L}\bm{b}_{1}+\tfrac{l_{i,2}}{L}\bm{b}_{2} and 𝒌j=lj,1L​𝒃1+lj,2L​𝒃2\bm{k}_{j}=\tfrac{l_{j,1}}{L}\bm{b}_{1}+\tfrac{l_{j,2}}{L}\bm{b}_{2} defined in Eq. 4, we stack them to form the vector

(li,1L,li,2L,lj,1L,lj,2L)∈[0,1)4.\bigl(\tfrac{l_{i,1}}{L},\tfrac{l_{i,2}}{L},\tfrac{l_{j,1}}{L},\tfrac{l_{j,2}}{L}\bigr)\in[0,1)^{4}. (24)

In each attention head, we then define a learnable continuous function fθ:ℝ4→ℝf_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{4}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} that maps each such pair of momenta to a scalar bias that represents how closely correlated they are. In general, this fθf_{\theta} can be parameterized as a standard NN, as in App. C. However, we can also explicitly incorporate our physical assumptions by using a carefully-chosen ansatz with a periodic basis, as is used in App. D and described below. Let Wr∈ℝm×2W_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 2} be a learnable matrix, where mm is a hyperparameter that determines the number of frequencies. Project each 𝒌i,𝒌j\bm{k}_{i},\bm{k}_{j}, separately:

𝒖i=Wr​[li,1Lli,2L]∈ℝm,𝒖j=Wr​[lj,1Llj,2L]∈ℝm.\bm{u}_{i}=W_{r}\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{l_{i,1}}{L}\\ \tfrac{l_{i,2}}{L}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\qquad\bm{u}_{j}=W_{r}\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{l_{j,1}}{L}\\ \tfrac{l_{j,2}}{L}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. (25)

We build periodic features

ϕ⁡(𝒌)≡cos⁡𝒖+sin⁡𝒖∈ℝm(applied elementwise),\bm{\phi}(\bm{k})\equiv\cos\bm{u}+\sin\bm{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\quad(\text{applied elementwise}), (26)

and take the difference

𝚫i​j=ϕ⁡(𝒌i)−ϕ⁡(𝒌j)∈ℝm.\bm{\Delta}_{ij}=\bm{\phi}(\bm{k}_{i})-\bm{\phi}(\bm{k}_{j})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. (27)

With a learnable vector of coefficients 𝑪∈ℝm\bm{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} (which is initially set to all 11’s before being optimized during training), we define a scalar, nonnegative “periodic distance” σi​j\sigma_{ij},

σi​j≡|⟨𝚫i​j,𝑪⟩|≥0,\sigma_{ij}\equiv\bigl|\langle\bm{\Delta}_{ij},\bm{C}\rangle\bigr|\geq 0, (28)

(here <,><,> means standard dot-product) and convert it to a decaying bias [129] fθf_{\theta}:

fθ​(𝒌i,𝒌j)≡exp⁡[−(σi​j+ε)p],ε=10−6,f_{\theta}(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{k}_{j})\equiv\exp\left[-\bigl(\sigma_{ij}+\varepsilon\bigr)^{p}\right],\qquad\varepsilon=10^{-6}\ , (29)

where p∈[0.5,3]p\in[0.5,3] is an exponent that serves as a practical stability constraint [112, 39, 9]. Repeating this process for each pair of momenta, we obtain a matrix B∈ℝL2×L2B\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times L^{2}}, where we define

Bi​j≡fθ​(𝒌i,𝒌j),i,j∈{1,…​L2}.B_{ij}\equiv f_{\theta}(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{k}_{j}),\quad i,j\in\{1,\dots L^{2}\}. (30)

Thus Bi​jB_{ij} acts as a smooth, periodic bias on the 1BZ [74, 144], which is shown as the Bias block in Fig. 2(d).

Besides the bias block, the attention head also involves the query QQ matrix, key KK matrix, value VV matrix, and Scalable Softmax. For each attention head h∈{1,…,Nhead}h\in\{1,\dots,N_{\text{head}}\} with NheadN_{\text{head}} the number of heads, we make matrices Q(h),K(h),V(h)∈ℝL2×dkQ^{(h)},K^{(h)},V^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times d_{k}} [137] by multiplying H(ℓ−1)H^{(\ell-1)} (the current layer’s input) with learnable matrices WQ(h),WK(h),WV(h)∈ℝD×dkW_{Q}^{(h)},\,W_{K}^{(h)},\,W_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{k}}, where dk≡D/Nheadd_{k}\equiv D/N_{\text{head}} is the width of each head and DD is the model width as defined in Sec. A.1.3. Then we have:

Q(h)=H(ℓ−1)​WQ(h),K(h)=H(ℓ−1)​WK(h),V(h)=H(ℓ−1)​WV(h).Q^{(h)}=H^{(\ell-1)}W_{Q}^{(h)},\qquad K^{(h)}=H^{(\ell-1)}W_{K}^{(h)},\qquad V^{(h)}=H^{(\ell-1)}W_{V}^{(h)}. (31)

With Bi​jB_{ij} from Eq. 30, define the pre-softmax logits [110, 137] as:

Λi​j(h)=τ⁡(⟨Qi(h),Kj(h)⟩+Bi​jdk),where ​τ≡s​log⁡(L2),\Lambda^{(h)}_{ij}=\tau\left(\frac{\big\langle Q^{(h)}_{i},K^{(h)}_{j}\big\rangle+B_{ij}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right),\qquad\text{where }\tau\equiv s\,\log\left(L^{2}\right)\ , (32)

and ss is a learnable parameter. (We use the notation of Qi,Ki,Q_{i},K_{i}, and ViV_{i} for the ithi^{\text{th}} row of Q,K,Q,K, and VV, respectively, with i∈{1,…​L2}i\in\{1,\dots L^{2}\}). Notice that Bi​j∈(0,1]B_{ij}\in(0,1] is large when 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i} and 𝒌j\bm{k}_{j} are close on 1BZ, so it adds extra preference to mix nearby momenta. Meanwhile, the multiplication by s​log⁡(L2)s\,\log\left(L^{2}\right) implements Scalable Softmax [103] to avoid the phenomenon of “attention fading”; that is, it ensures that for a large number of 𝒌\bm{k} points [110], the maximum value of the attention weights does not drop to 00, which could otherwise hinder the NN’s capacity for length generalization. The attention weights and head outputs are

Ai​j(h)=eτ​Λi​j(h)∑m=1L2eτ​Λi​m(h),∑jAi​j(h)=1,Ai​j(h)>0.A_{ij}^{(h)}=\frac{e^{\tau\Lambda_{ij}^{(h)}}}{\sum_{m=1}^{L^{2}}e^{\tau\Lambda_{im}^{(h)}}},\qquad\sum_{j}A_{ij}^{(h)}=1,\quad A_{ij}^{(h)}>0. (33)

i.e., Softmax [8] is applied here (row-wise normalization that turns attention scores into positive weights summing to 11). Then,

𝒛i(h)=∑j=1L2Ai​j(h)​Vj(h)∈ℝdk.\bm{z}^{(h)}_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{L^{2}}A^{(h)}_{ij}\,V^{(h)}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}. (34)

We can stack all the 𝒛i′​s\bm{z}_{i}^{\prime}s constructed in this way to form a matrix:

Z(h)=[𝒛1(h)𝒛L2(h)]∈ℝL2×dk.Z^{(h)}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{z}_{1}^{(h)}\\ \vdots\\ \bm{z}_{L^{2}}^{(h)}\\ \end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times d_{k}}. (35)

Therefore, a summary of the attention head we just discussed in Eq. 31-Eq. 33 is the following (see the red box in Fig. 2):

AttentionHead(h)​(H(ℓ−1))≔Z(h)with{Q(h)=H(ℓ−1)WQ(h),K(h)=H(ℓ−1)WK(h),V(h)=H(ℓ−1)WV(h),Λ(h)i​j=τ(⟨Qi(h),Kj(h)⟩+Bi​jdk),where τ≡slog(L2),Ai​j(h)=eτ​Λi​j(h)∑m=1L2eτ​Λi​m(h),∑jAi​j(h)=1,Ai​j(h)>0,Z(h)=A(h)​V(h).\mathrm{AttentionHead}^{(h)}\big(H^{(\ell-1)}\big)\coloneqq Z^{(h)}\quad\text{with}\quad\begin{cases}Q^{(h)}=H^{(\ell-1)}W_{Q}^{(h)},\quad K^{(h)}=H^{(\ell-1)}W_{K}^{(h)},\quad V^{(h)}=H^{(\ell-1)}W_{V}^{(h)},\\ \Lambda^{(h)}_{ij}=\tau\left(\frac{\big\langle Q^{(h)}_{i},\,K^{(h)}_{j}\big\rangle+B_{ij}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right),\text{where }\tau\equiv s\log\left(L^{2}\right),\\ A_{ij}^{(h)}=\frac{e^{\tau\Lambda_{ij}^{(h)}}}{\sum_{m=1}^{L^{2}}e^{\tau\Lambda_{im}^{(h)}}},\quad\sum_{j}A_{ij}^{(h)}=1,\quad A_{ij}^{(h)}>0,\\ Z^{(h)}=A^{(h)}V^{(h)}.\end{cases} (36)

Finally, the Nhead≥1N_{\text{head}}\geq 1 attention heads form an attention block. Parameters are not shared between different attention heads (even if they are in the same attention block), (i.e., each individual attention head has its own set of learnable parameters which are optimized independently from the others). For all i∈{1,…​L2}i\in\{1,\dots L^{2}\}, we concatenate (i.e.“stack”) the output vectors 𝒛i(h)∈ℝdk\bm{z}^{(h)}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} from each attention head into a single vector of size Nhead​dk=DN_{\text{head}}d_{k}=D:

Concat⁡(Z(1),…,Z(Nhead))=[Z(1)Z(2)⋯Z(Nhead)]∈ℝL2×D.\mathrm{Concat}\big(Z^{(1)},\ldots,Z^{(N_{\text{head}})}\big)=\big[Z^{(1)}\ \ Z^{(2)}\ \ \cdots\ \ Z^{(N_{\text{head}})}\,\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{\,L^{2}\times D}. (37)

and then apply an output linear map with learnable parameters WO∈ℝD×D,𝒃O∈ℝDW_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D},\bm{b}_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}:

Z=Concat⁡(Z(1),…,Z(Nhead))​WO+𝟏​𝒃O⊤,{Z}=\operatorname{Concat}\big({Z}^{(1)},\ldots,{Z}^{(N_{\text{head}})}\big)\,W_{O}+\bm{1}\bm{b}_{O}^{\top}, (38)

and here 𝟏\bm{1} is a length-L2L^{2} column of ones. This mixes information across heads and returns to the model width DD.

A.1.5 Dropout, Layer Normalization, and FFN

We now discuss the dropout, layer normalization, and FFN in each each attention layer (we first introduced them in Sec. A.1.3) as shown in Fig. 2(b).

Applying Dropout\operatorname{Dropout} to a vector or matrix means that we randomly set each element of the vector or matrix to zero with a probability pp or keep it with a probability of 1−p1-p [133]. We apply dropout to the attention output 𝒁\bm{Z} (Eq. 39), add the result to the layer input H(ℓ−1)H^{(\ell-1)} (Eq. 40), and then apply LayerNorm per 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i}:

Z^=Dropout⁡(Z),where ​Dropout⁡(Z)i​j=mi​j​Zi​j1−p,mi​j∼Bernoulli⁡(1−p),\hat{{Z}}=\operatorname{Dropout}({Z}),\qquad\text{where }\operatorname{Dropout}({Z})_{ij}=\frac{m_{ij}{Z}_{ij}}{1-p},\quad m_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-p), (39)
𝑼i=LayerNorm⁡(Hi(ℓ−1)+𝒁^i),U∈ℝL2×D.\bm{U}_{i}=\operatorname{LayerNorm}\big(H_{i}^{(\ell-1)}+\hat{\bm{Z}}_{i}\big),\quad{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times D}. (40)

Here LayerNorm is applied independently to each 𝑼i∈ℝD\bm{U}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, and is defined as follows: define the mean and variance over d=1,…,Dd=1,\dots,D:

μi≡1D​∑d=1DUi,d,σi2≡1D​∑d=1D(Ui,d−μi)2,\mu_{i}\equiv\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}U_{i,d},\qquad\sigma_{i}^{2}\equiv\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\big(U_{i,d}-\mu_{i}\big)^{2}, (41)

then, with learnable parameters 𝜸,𝜷∈ℝD\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and a small ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we set

LayerNorm⁡(𝑼i)≡γ⊙𝑼i−μi​𝟏σi2+ϵ+β∈ℝD,\mathrm{LayerNorm}(\bm{U}_{i})\equiv\gamma\odot\frac{\bm{U}_{i}-\mu_{i}\bm{1}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{i}^{2}+\epsilon}}+\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (42)

where ⊙\odot is the element-wise product. Namely,

[LayerNorm(Ui)]d=γdUi,d−μiσi2+ϵ+βd,d=1,…,D.\big[\mathrm{LayerNorm}(U_{i})\big]_{d}=\gamma_{d}\frac{U_{i,d}-\mu_{i}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{i}^{2}+\epsilon}}+\beta_{d},\qquad d=1,\ldots,D. (43)

For every 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i}, take its current vector 𝑼i∈ℝD\bm{U}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and apply a learned linear map which increases the dimension to a larger width DffD_{\mathrm{ff}}, to get 𝑭i=W1​𝑼i+𝒃1\bm{F}_{i}=W_{1}\bm{U}_{i}+\bm{b}_{1} with W1∈ℝD×DffW_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D_{\mathrm{ff}}} and 𝒃1∈ℝDff\bm{b}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\mathrm{ff}}}:

F=U​W1+1​𝒃1⊤∈ℝL2×Dff.F=UW_{1}+\textbf{1}\bm{b}_{1}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times D_{\text{ff}}}. (44)

Apply the GELU (“Gaussian Error Linear Unit”[49]) element-wise to FF, which smoothly gates each component of FF: small negative values are damped, large positive values pass through almost linearly. It is written using the error function erf\operatorname{erf}, then mapped back from the hidden width to the model width:

U^=W2​GELU​(F)+1​𝒃2⊤∈ℝL2×DwhereGELU⁡(F)≡F2​(𝟏+erf⁡(F2)),\widehat{U}=W_{2}\,\mathrm{GELU}(F)+\textbf{1}\bm{b}_{2}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times D}\quad\text{where}\quad\mathrm{GELU}(F)\equiv\frac{F}{2}\left(\bm{1}+\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{F}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right), (45)

with W2∈ℝDff×DW_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\mathrm{ff}}\times D}, 𝒃2∈ℝD\bm{b}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, and 𝟏∈ℝL2\bm{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}} (column of ones). Then,

H(ℓ)=LayerNorm⁡(𝑼+Dropout⁡(𝑼^)).H^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{LayerNorm}\left(\bm{U}+\mathrm{Dropout}(\widehat{\bm{U}})\right). (46)

Eq. 45 is labeled as FFN in Fig. 2.

A.2 SIREN with Custom Loss Function

Alternatively, rather than learning a map from a random initial n-RDM to a final n-RDM, we may treat the task purely as interpolation: we learn a continuous function Φ\Phi (the interpolant) represented by a NN that takes momentum–space coordinates 𝒌\bm{k} (or normalized coordinates 𝒗∈[−1,1]2\bm{v}\in[-1,1]^{2}, see Eq. 48) as input, and outputs a matrix O𝒒​(𝒌i)O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}_{i}) representing the n-RDM, e.g. Φ⁡(𝒌)≈Oα​α′𝒒​(𝒌)\Phi(\bm{k})\approx O^{\bm{q}}_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}(\bm{k}) (or Re/ImOα​α′𝒒​(𝒌)\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}/\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}\,O^{\bm{q}}_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}(\bm{k}) when training the real/imaginary parts separately). The explicit structure is in Sec. A.2.3. One way to achieve this interpolation is the SIREN architecture. In the following, we will discuss it using the example of fixed-𝒒\bm{q} 11-RDM that only depends on one 𝒌\bm{k}. Nevertheless, the discussion holds for a matrix that depends on more than one Bloch momenta, as shown in App. B.

A.2.1 physical set-up

We keep the BZ discretization of Eq. 4. All nn-RDM are defined as in Sec. A.1.1. As discussed in Sec. A.1.1, we focus on considering the fixed-𝒒\bm{q} 1-RDMs (O𝒌,α​α′𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}) over BZ with a shape of L×L×ξ×ξL\times L\times\xi\times\xi. The overall goal of the SIREN [131] approach is to train one continuous function Φ⁡(kx,ky)\Phi(k_{x},k_{y}) that predicts each 1-RDM block over the BZ. In particular, we train a function Φ⁡(kx,ky)\Phi(k_{x},k_{y}) per (α,α′)(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}) and per real/imaginary part of O𝒌,α​α′𝒒O^{\bm{q}}_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}} if needed, such that

Φ⁡(𝒌)≈Re[O𝒌,α​α′𝒒]orIm[O𝒌,α​α′𝒒].\Phi(\bm{k})\approx\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}\left[O^{\bm{q}}_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}\right]\quad\text{or}\quad\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}\left[O^{\bm{q}}_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}\right]. (47)

(In practice, both the Hubbard (App. D) and the Richardson (App. B) model exhibit a vanishing imaginary part, so we only consider the real part for training in those cases.) Stacking all different Φ\Phi for all different values of (α,α′)(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}) reconstructs O𝒒​(𝒌)O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}). We will train on smaller BZ grids, and then evaluate Φ\Phi on denser BZ grids.

A.2.2 NN input

For an L×LL\times L BZ with 𝒌i\bm{k}_{i} from Eq. 4, we define the normalized coordinate

𝒗⁡(𝒌)≡(2​ℓ1L−1,2​ℓ2L−1)∈[−1,1]2,for ​𝒌=ℓ1L​𝒃1+ℓ2L​𝒃2.\bm{v}(\bm{k})\equiv\Big(2\,\tfrac{\ell_{1}}{L}-1,2\,\tfrac{\ell_{2}}{L}-1\Big)\in[-1,1]^{2},\quad\text{for }\bm{k}=\tfrac{\ell_{1}}{L}\bm{b}_{1}+\tfrac{\ell_{2}}{L}\bm{b}_{2}. (48)

For each fixed (α,α′)(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}), evaluate Re[O𝒒​(𝒌)]​ and ​Im[O𝒒​(𝒌)]​ for all ​𝒌.\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k})]\text{ and }\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}[O^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k})]\ \text{ for all }\bm{k}. To enforce periodicity at the boundaries, extend each to a wrapped array

Re[O~𝒒],Im[O~𝒒]∈ℝ(L+1)×(L+1)\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[\widetilde{O}^{\bm{q}}],\ \mathop{\mathrm{Im}}[\widetilde{O}^{\bm{q}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{(L+1)\times(L+1)} (49)

by repeating the first row and column:

O~m,n𝒒≡OmmodL,nmodL𝒒,m,n∈{0,1,…,L}\tilde{O}^{\bm{q}}_{m,n}\equiv O^{\bm{q}}_{\,m\bmod L,n\bmod L},\qquad m,n\in\{0,1,\dots,L\} (50)

So O~𝒒\widetilde{O}^{\bm{q}} is just O𝒒O^{\bm{q}} with its first row/column copied to the end—this “closes” the matrix at finite LL.

A.2.3 SIREN architecture

Given input to our NN in the form of Eq. 48, we build one SIREN [131] (depicted in Fig. 3) to predict each block of the 1-RDM respectively (e.g., Re[O⁡(𝒌)]\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[O(\bm{k})] or Im[O⁡(𝒌)]\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}[O(\bm{k})]). Each SIREN has 4 hidden sine layers: 𝒉1,𝒉2,𝒉3,𝒉4\bm{h}_{1},\bm{h}_{2},\bm{h}_{3},\bm{h}_{4}, followed by a final linear layer. Explicitly,

𝒉1​(𝒗)\displaystyle\bm{h}_{1}(\bm{v}) =sin(6(W1𝒗+𝒃1))∈ℝdH,\displaystyle=\sin\big(6\,(W_{1}\bm{v}+\bm{b}_{1})\big)\quad\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}}, (51)
𝒉2​(𝒗)\displaystyle\bm{h}_{2}(\bm{v}) =sin(30(W2𝒉1(𝒗)+𝒃2))∈ℝdH,\displaystyle=\sin\big(30\,(W_{2}\bm{h}_{1}(\bm{v})+\bm{b}_{2})\big)\quad\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}},
𝒉3​(𝒗)\displaystyle\bm{h}_{3}(\bm{v}) =sin(30(W3𝒉2(𝒗)+𝒃3))∈ℝdH,\displaystyle=\sin\big(30\,(W_{3}\bm{h}_{2}(\bm{v})+\bm{b}_{3})\big)\quad\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}},
𝒉4​(𝒗)\displaystyle\bm{h}_{4}(\bm{v}) =sin(30(W4𝒉3(𝒗)+𝒃4))∈ℝdH,\displaystyle=\sin\big(30\,(W_{4}\bm{h}_{3}(\bm{v})+\bm{b}_{4})\big)\quad\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}},
Φθ​(𝒗)\displaystyle\Phi_{\theta}(\bm{v}) =𝒘⊤𝒉4(𝒗)+bout∈ℝ.\displaystyle=\bm{w}^{\top}\bm{h}_{4}(\bm{v})+b_{\text{out}}\quad\in\mathbb{R}.

where

𝒗∈ℝ2,W1∈ℝdH×2,W2,W3,W4∈ℝdH×dH,𝒃1,𝒃2,𝒃3,𝒃4∈ℝdH,𝒘∈ℝdH,bout∈ℝ.\displaystyle\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\quad W_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}\times 2},W_{2},W_{3},W_{4}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}\times d_{H}},\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2},\bm{b}_{3},\bm{b}_{4}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}},\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}},b_{\text{out}}\in\mathbb{R}. (52)

Eq. 51 maps a BZ coordinate from Eq. 48, 𝒗=(vx,vy)∈[−1,1]2\bm{v}=(v_{x},v_{y})\in[-1,1]^{2}, to a scalar Φθ​(𝒗)∈ℝ\Phi_{\theta}(\bm{v})\in\mathbb{R} that predicts the corresponding element of either Re[O𝒒]​(𝒌i)\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[O^{\bm{q}}](\bm{k}_{i}) or Im[O𝒒]​(𝒌i)\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}[O^{\bm{q}}](\bm{k}_{i}). The layer widths are: d0=2d_{0}=2 for the input vector 𝒗\bm{v} (from Eq. 48), and d1=d2=d3=d4=dHd_{1}=d_{2}=d_{3}=d_{4}=d_{H} for the hidden layers (h1,2,3,4h_{1,2,3,4} in Eq. 51) for which we usually select dH∈[256,800]d_{H}\in[256,800]. We choose sines because they naturally model smooth, periodic patterns across the BZ. Additionally, to keep gradients healthy, we incorporate a special weight initialization scheme [131]: define W∼𝒰⁡(a,b)W\sim\mathcal{U}(a,b) to mean “sample uniformly at random between aa and bb.” Here W∼𝒰W\sim\mathcal{U} denotes element-wise initialization: each entry Wi​jW_{ij} is drawn independently from 𝒰⁡(a,b)\mathcal{U}(a,b). Then we initialize the weights in Eq. 51 with:

W1∼𝒰⁡(−1d0,1d0),and ​w⊤,Wℓ∼𝒰⁡(−6/dH30,6/dH30)​ elementwise, 2≤ℓ≤4.W_{1}\sim\mathcal{U}\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{d_{0}},\tfrac{1}{d_{0}}\Bigr),\qquad\text{and }w^{\top},W_{\ell}\sim\mathcal{U}\Bigl(-\tfrac{\sqrt{6/d_{H}}}{30},\tfrac{\sqrt{6/d_{H}}}{30}\Bigr)\text{ elementwise, }\quad 2\leq\ell\leq 4. (53)

The full model can then be written as Φθ\Phi_{\theta}, where θ\theta represents all the tunable parameters mentioned above.

A.2.4 Datasets, standardization, and evaluation grids

For Re[O~𝒒]∈ℝ(L+1)×(L+1)\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[\tilde{O}^{\bm{q}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{(L+1)\times(L+1)} defined in Eq. 49 , we compute the mean and standard deviation over all entries:

μ=mean⁡(Re[O~𝒒]),σ=std⁡(Re[O~𝒒]),\mu=\mathrm{mean}(\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[\tilde{O}^{\bm{q}}]),\qquad\sigma=\mathrm{std}(\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[\tilde{O}^{\bm{q}}]), (54)

and form the standardized version of O~𝒒:\widetilde{O}^{\bm{q}}:

ZL≡Re[O~𝒒]−μσ∈ℝ(L+1)×(L+1).Z_{L}\equiv\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}[\tilde{O}^{\bm{q}}]-\mu}{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{(L+1)\times(L+1)}. (55)

A similar standardization procedure applies for Im[O~𝒒]\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}[\tilde{O}^{\bm{q}}]. For evaluation on larger LL, we use the same μ\mu and σ\sigma (computed from the O𝒒O^{\bm{q}} used for training) to normalize the data. Also notice that the unstandardized SIREN predictions for the target channel can be recovered after training by reversing Eq. 55. Each input point is a normalized BZ coordinate ν∈[−1,1]2\nu\in[-1,1]^{2} (see Eq. 48). Define the coordinate grid XL≡{𝒗(𝒌i​j):i,j=0,…,L}⊂[−1,1](L+1)×(L+1)×2,𝒌i​j≡iL𝒃1+jL𝒃2.X_{L}\equiv\{\bm{v}(\bm{k}_{ij}):i,j=0,\ldots,L\}\subset[-1,1]^{(L+1)\times(L+1)\times 2},\quad\bm{k}_{ij}\equiv\tfrac{i}{L}\bm{b}_{1}+\tfrac{j}{L}\bm{b}_{2}. Our training data thus consists of the set of input coordinates XL∈[−1,1](L+1)×(L+1)×2X_{L}\in[-1,1]^{(L+1)\times(L+1)\times 2} and the normalized values ZLZ_{L}.

When calculating the loss, we also evaluate SIREN on a L′×L′L^{\prime}\times L^{\prime} mesh with L′>LL^{\prime}>L and output ZL′∈[−1,1](L′+1)×(L′+1)×2Z_{L^{\prime}}\in[-1,1]^{(L^{\prime}+1)\times(L^{\prime}+1)\times 2}, as seen in Sec. A.2.5. However, we will eventually downsample the ZL′Z_{L^{\prime}} back to L×LL\times L mesh to compare to the training data. In this process, we do not use any true final RDMs on the L′×L′L^{\prime}\times L^{\prime} mesh as training data, since doing so would defeat our entire purpose of generalizing to larger system sizes.

A.2.5 Loss function

Define Φθ:[−1,1]2→ℝ\Phi_{\theta}:[-1,1]^{2}\to\mathbb{R} to be the SIREN we constructed in Sec. A.2.3 with tunable parameters denoted as θ\theta, which takes a normalized BZ coordinate 𝒗⁡(𝒌)∈[−1,1]2\bm{v}(\bm{k})\in[-1,1]^{2} as input and outputs a scalar prediction for the corresponding element of the chosen 1-RDM block:

Z^​(𝒌)≡Φθ​(𝒗⁡(𝒌)),\widehat{Z}(\bm{k})\equiv\Phi_{\theta}\bigl(\bm{v}(\bm{k})\bigr), (56)

For small-mesh MSE,

ℒsmall​(θ)=1(L+1)2​∑𝒗∈XL(Z^​(XL)​[𝒗]−ZL​[𝒗])2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{small}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{(L+1)^{2}}\sum_{\bm{v}\in X_{L}}\Big(\widehat{Z}(X_{L})[\bm{v}]-Z_{L}[\bm{v}]\Big)^{2}. (57)

Let GG be any finite symmetry subgroup of the symmetry group of the system acting on normalized BZ coordinates 𝒗∈[−1,1]2\bm{v}\in[-1,1]^{2} (e.g., rotations/reflections of the square). Define the symmetrization operator SGS_{G} by averaging over the group action. For example, for a square lattice we take G=D4G=D_{4} (order 88, consisting of four rotations 0∘,90∘,180∘,270∘0^{\circ},90^{\circ},180^{\circ},270^{\circ} and four reflections across the two axes and two diagonals). Let ζ\zeta be a fixed downsampler (e.g. bilinear or bicubic interpolation [61, 102]), which is effectively a classical algorithm used to interpolate the SIREN predictions on the denser coordinate mesh XL′X_{L^{\prime}} back to the training system size. This allows us to control behavior at finer scales, without the need for additional training data (e.g. ZL′Z_{L^{\prime}}) from the larger system. As such, we evaluate the SIREN on the dense grid XL′X_{L^{\prime}}, symmetrize, and then downsample back down to XLX_{L}:

Z^↓​(XL)≡ζ⁡(𝒮G​[Z^​(XL′)]→XL),\widehat{Z}^{\downarrow}(X_{L})\equiv\zeta\big(\,\mathcal{S}_{G}[\widehat{Z}(X_{L^{\prime}})]\to X_{L}\big), (58)
ℒcons​(θ)=1(L+1)2​∑𝒗∈XL(Z^↓​(XL)​[𝒗]−ZL​[𝒗])2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{(L+1)^{2}}\sum_{\bm{v}\in X_{L}}\Big(\widehat{Z}^{\downarrow}(X_{L})[\bm{v}]-Z_{L}[\bm{v}]\Big)^{2}. (59)

(Note that for the Richardson model in Sec. B.2, we employ a slightly different technique to learn the symmetry group during training; see Eq. 195 for details.) Randomly sample NN points U={ui}i=1N⊂[−1,1]2U=\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\subset[-1,1]^{2}. With ∇u\nabla_{u} the gradient and Hessu\mathrm{Hess}_{u} the Hessian w.r.t. uu, and with ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} the ℓ1\ell^{1} norm and ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} the Frobenius norm:

𝒫TV​(θ)≡1N​∑i=1N‖∇uΦθ​(ui)‖1,𝒫FH​(θ)≡1N​∑i=1N‖Hessu​Φθ​(ui)‖F.\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\theta)\equiv\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\|\nabla_{u}\Phi_{\theta}(u_{i})\big\|_{1},\qquad\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{FH}}(\theta)\equiv\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\|\mathrm{Hess}_{u}\Phi_{\theta}(u_{i})\big\|_{F}\ . (60)

The total loss is:

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒsmall​(θ)+ℒcons​(θ)+λ​𝒫​(θ),𝒫∈{𝒫TV,𝒫FH, 0},\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{small}}(\theta)+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\theta)+\lambda\,\mathcal{P}(\theta),\qquad\mathcal{P}\in\{\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{TV}},\,\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{FH}},\,0\}, (61)

with λ∈[10−7, 10−5]\lambda\in[10^{-7},\,10^{-5}] in practice. We then take the gradient of ℒ\mathcal{L} w.r.t. θ\theta and train the SIREN using the Adam optimizer [64]. For all trainings using a SIREN-based NN in this paper, we set the constant learning rate for the optimizer equal to 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}.

1g+∑𝒌12​ε𝒌−Eμ−∑ν≠μ2Eν−Eμ=0,μ=1,…,M.\frac{1}{g}+\sum_{\bm{k}}\frac{1}{2\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu}}-\sum_{\nu\neq\mu}\frac{2}{E_{\nu}-E_{\mu}}=0,\qquad\mu=1,\dots,M.\ (111)

as claimed [26].

After obtaining the Richardson equations, it is convenient to introduce the Jacobian matrix with respect to the rapidities:

Gμ​μ\displaystyle G_{\mu\mu} =∂Rμ∂Eμ=∑𝒌∂∂Eμ​(2​ε𝒌−Eμ)−1−∑ν≠μ2​∂∂Eμ​(Eν−Eμ)−1\displaystyle=\frac{\partial R_{\mu}}{\partial E_{\mu}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}\frac{\partial}{\partial E_{\mu}}(2\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})^{-1}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\neq\mu\end{subarray}}2\frac{\partial}{\partial E_{\mu}}(E_{\nu}-E_{\mu})^{-1} (114)
=∑𝒌[−(2ε𝒌−Eμ)−2⋅(−1)]−2∑ν≠μM[−(Eν−Eμ)−2⋅(−1)]=∑𝒌1(2​ε𝒌−Eμ)2−2∑ν≠μM1(Eν−Eμ)2.\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}}\left[-(2\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})^{-2}\cdot(-1)\right]-2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\neq\mu\end{subarray}}^{M}\left[-(E_{\nu}-E_{\mu})^{-2}\cdot(-1)\right]=\sum_{\bm{k}}\frac{1}{(2\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})^{2}}-2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\neq\mu\end{subarray}}^{M}\frac{1}{(E_{\nu}-E_{\mu})^{2}}. (115)

Gμ​ν={∑𝒌1(2​ε𝒌−Eμ)2−2​∑λ≠μ1(Eλ−Eμ)2,ν=μ,2(Eν−Eμ)2,ν≠μ.G_{\mu\nu}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}}\frac{1}{(2\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})^{2}}-2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\neq\mu\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{(E_{\lambda}-E_{\mu})^{2}},&\nu=\mu,\\ \displaystyle\frac{2}{(E_{\nu}-E_{\mu})^{2}},&\nu\neq\mu.\end{cases} (116)

This is called Gaudin matrix [26], which will be useful later in Sec. B.1.2 when expressing correlation functions.

B.1.2 Pair–Pair Correlators: Exact Formula

With the Cooper-pair operator Ak†A_{k}^{\dagger} and AkA_{k} defined in Eq. 81, for a general many‑body state, the pair–pair correlator is

C~𝒌​𝒌′≡⟨A𝒌†​A𝒌′⟩−⟨A𝒌†⟩​⟨A𝒌′⟩,\widetilde{C}_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}\equiv\big\langle A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\big\rangle-\big\langle A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\big\rangle\big\langle A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\big\rangle\ , (117)

where ⟨…⟩\big\langle...\big\rangle is the average with respect to the state of interest. In the Richardson model we work with number‑conserving eigenstates |Ψ2​M⟩|\Psi_{2M}\rangle (fixed particle number 2​M2M). Since A𝒌A_{\bm{k}} lowers particle number by two, A𝒌​|Ψ2​M⟩A_{\bm{k}}|\Psi_{2M}\rangle lies in the 2​M−22M-2 sector and is orthogonal to |Ψ2​M⟩|\Psi_{2M}\rangle, hence

⟨A𝒌⟩=⟨Ψ2​M|A𝒌|Ψ2​M⟩=0.\big\langle A_{\bm{k}}\big\rangle=\langle\Psi_{2M}|A_{\bm{k}}|\Psi_{2M}\rangle=0. (118)

Therefore the connected and full correlators coincide,

C~𝒌​𝒌′=⟨A𝒌†​A𝒌′⟩.\widetilde{C}_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}=\big\langle A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\big\rangle. (119)

Writing out Ak†A_{k}^{\dagger} and Ak′A_{k^{\prime}},

⟨A𝒌†​A𝒌′⟩=⟨c𝒌↑†​c−𝒌↓†​c−𝒌′↓​c𝒌′↑⟩,\big\langle A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\big\rangle=\big\langle c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}\downarrow}c_{-\bm{k}^{\prime}\downarrow}c_{\bm{k}^{\prime}\uparrow}\big\rangle, (120)

which is exactly the Cooper‑channel combination of the 2-RDM defined in Eq. 1, i.e.

C𝒌​𝒌′≡C~𝒌​𝒌′=O𝒌↑,−𝒌↓,𝒌′↑,−𝒌′↓.C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}\equiv\widetilde{C}_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}=O_{\bm{k}\uparrow,-\bm{k}\downarrow,\bm{k}^{\prime}\uparrow,-\bm{k}^{\prime}\downarrow}. (121)

(For U(1)–breaking mean‑field states we may have ⟨A𝒌⟩≠0\langle A_{\bm{k}}\rangle\neq 0, in which case the connected correlator (117) differs from the full 22‑RDM matrix element by ⟨A𝒌†⟩​⟨A𝒌′⟩\langle A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\rangle\langle A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\rangle; in our number‑conserving case, (118) ensures they are identical.)

Now we derive a general expression of ⟨Ψ2​M|A𝒌†​A𝒌′|Ψ2​M⟩\langle\Psi_{2M}|A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}|\Psi_{2M}\rangle. Let’s start from

A𝒌′|Ψ2​M⟩=A𝒌′(∏ϵ=1MBϵ†)|0⟩.A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\lvert\Psi_{2M}\rangle=A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\left(\prod_{\epsilon=1}^{M}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle. (122)

Because A𝒌′|0⟩=0A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\lvert 0\rangle=0, we can commute A𝒌′A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}} through the product and keep only commutators:

A𝒌′(∏ϵ=1MBϵ†)|0⟩\displaystyle A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\left(\prod_{\epsilon=1}^{M}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle =∏ϵ=1MBϵ†A𝒌′|0⟩+∑μ=1M(∏ϵ<μBϵ†)[A𝒌′,Bμ†](∏ϵ>μBϵ†)|0⟩\displaystyle=\prod_{\epsilon=1}^{M}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\lvert 0\rangle+\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\left(\prod_{\epsilon<\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\bigl[A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},B_{\mu}^{\dagger}\bigr]\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle (123)
=∑μ=1M(∏ϵ<μBϵ†)[A𝒌′,Bμ†](∏ϵ>μBϵ†)|0⟩.\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\left(\prod_{\epsilon<\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\bigl[A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},B_{\mu}^{\dagger}\bigr]\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle. (124)

We can compute the commutator using Bμ†=∑𝒑ϕμ​(𝒑)​A𝒑†B_{\mu}^{\dagger}=\sum_{\bm{p}}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{p})A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger} and [A𝒌′,A𝒑†]=δ𝒌′​𝒑​(1−N𝒌′)[A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}]=\delta_{\bm{k}^{\prime}\bm{p}}(1-N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}):

[A𝒌′,Bμ†]=∑𝒑ϕμ​(𝒑)​[A𝒌′,A𝒑†]=∑𝒑ϕμ​(𝒑)​δ𝒌′​𝒑​(1−N𝒌′)=ϕμ​(𝒌′)​(1−N𝒌′).\bigl[A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},B_{\mu}^{\dagger}\bigr]=\sum_{\bm{p}}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{p})\bigl[A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}\bigr]=\sum_{\bm{p}}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{p})\delta_{\bm{k}^{\prime}\bm{p}}(1-N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}})=\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})(1-N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}). (125)

Therefore,

A𝒌′|Ψ2​M⟩\displaystyle A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\lvert\Psi_{2M}\rangle =∑μ=1Mϕμ(𝒌′)(∏ϵ<μBϵ†)(1−N𝒌′)(∏ϵ>μBϵ†)|0⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon<\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)(1-N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}})\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle (126)
=∑μ=1Mϕμ(𝒌′)(∏ϵ<μBϵ†)[(∏ϵ>μBϵ†)(1−N𝒌′)|0⟩+∑ν>μ(∏μ<ϵ<νBϵ†)[1−N𝒌′,Bν†](∏ϵ>νBϵ†)|0⟩],\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon<\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\Biggl[\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)(1-N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}})\lvert 0\rangle+\sum_{\nu>\mu}\left(\prod_{\mu<\epsilon<\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\bigl[1-N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},B_{\nu}^{\dagger}\bigr]\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle\Biggr], (127)

where [N𝒌′,Bν†]=∑𝒑ϕν​(𝒑)​[N𝒌′,A𝒑†]=2​ϕν​(𝒌′)​A𝒌′†,\bigl[N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},B_{\nu}^{\dagger}\bigr]=\sum_{\bm{p}}\phi_{\nu}(\bm{p})\bigl[N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}\bigr]=2\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}, using Eq. 83, so [1−N𝒌′,Bν†]=−2​ϕν​(𝒌′)​A𝒌′†\bigl[1-N_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},B_{\nu}^{\dagger}\bigr]=-2\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}. Thus,

A𝒌′|Ψ2​M⟩\displaystyle A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\lvert\Psi_{2M}\rangle =∑μ=1Mϕμ(𝒌′)(∏ϵ<μBϵ†)[(∏ϵ>μBϵ†)|0⟩−∑ν>μ(∏μ<ϵ<νBϵ†)2ϕν(k′)Ak′†(∏ϵ>νBϵ†)|0⟩]\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon<\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\Biggl[\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle-\sum_{\nu>\mu}\left(\prod_{\mu<\epsilon<\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)2\,\phi_{\nu}(k^{\prime})\,A_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle\Biggr] (128)
=∑μ=1Mϕμ(𝒌′)(∏ϵ≠μBϵ†)|0⟩−∑μ=1Mϕμ(𝒌′)(∏ϵ<μBϵ†)∑ν>μ(∏μ<ϵ<νBϵ†)2ϕν(𝒌′)A𝒌′†(∏ϵ>νBϵ†)|0⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon\neq\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle-\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon<\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\sum_{\nu>\mu}\left(\prod_{\mu<\epsilon<\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)2\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle (129)
=∑μ=1Mϕμ(𝒌′)(∏ϵ≠μBϵ†)|0⟩−2A𝒌′†∑μ=1M∑ν>μϕμ(𝒌′)ϕν(𝒌′)(∏ϵ<μBϵ†)(∏μ<ϵ<νBϵ†)(∏ϵ>νBϵ†)|0⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon\neq\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle-2A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\sum_{\nu>\mu}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\,\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon<\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\left(\prod_{\mu<\epsilon<\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\left(\prod_{\epsilon>\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle (130)
=∑μ=1Mϕμ(𝒌′)(∏ϵ≠μBϵ†)|0⟩−2A𝒌′†∑1≤μ<ν≤Mϕμ(𝒌′)ϕν(𝒌′)(∏ϵ≠μ,νBϵ†)|0⟩.\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon\neq\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle-2A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\sum_{1\leq\mu<\nu\leq M}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\left(\prod_{\epsilon\neq\mu,\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle. (131)

Define the shorthand:

|Ψ(μ)⟩≡(∏ϵ≠μBϵ†)|0⟩,|Ψ(μ​ν)⟩≡(∏ϵ≠μ,νBϵ†)|0⟩,⟨Ψ(ρ)|≡⟨0|(∏ω≠ρBω),⟨Ψ(ρ​σ)|≡⟨0|(∏ω≠ρ,σBω).\lvert\Psi^{(\mu)}\rangle\equiv\left(\prod_{\epsilon\neq\mu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle,\quad\lvert\Psi^{(\mu\nu)}\rangle\equiv\left(\prod_{\epsilon\neq\mu,\nu}B_{\epsilon}^{\dagger}\right)\lvert 0\rangle,\quad\langle\Psi^{(\rho)}\rvert\equiv\langle 0\rvert\left(\prod_{\omega\neq\rho}B_{\omega}\right),\quad\langle\Psi^{(\rho\sigma)}\rvert\equiv\langle 0\rvert\left(\prod_{\omega\neq\rho,\sigma}B_{\omega}\right). (132)

Therefore,

⟨Ψ2​M|A𝒌†​A𝒌′|Ψ2​M⟩\displaystyle\langle\Psi_{2M}|A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}|\Psi_{2M}\rangle =⟨Ψ2​M|A𝒌†[∑μϕμ(𝒌′)|Ψ(μ)⟩−2A𝒌′†∑μ<νϕμ(𝒌′)ϕν(𝒌′)|Ψ(μ​ν)⟩]\displaystyle=\langle\Psi_{2M}\lvert A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\Bigl[\sum_{\mu}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\lvert\Psi^{(\mu)}\rangle-2A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\sum_{\mu<\nu}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\lvert\Psi^{(\mu\nu)}\rangle\Bigr] (133)
=∑μϕμ​(𝒌′)​⟨Ψ2​M​|A𝒌†|​Ψ(μ)⟩−2​∑μ<νϕμ​(𝒌′)​ϕν​(𝒌′)​⟨Ψ2​M​|A𝒌†​A𝒌′†|​Ψ(μ​ν)⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\langle\Psi_{2M}\lvert A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\rvert\Psi^{(\mu)}\rangle-2\sum_{\mu<\nu}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\langle\Psi_{2M}\lvert A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rvert\Psi^{(\mu\nu)}\rangle (134)
=∑μϕμ​(𝒌′)​F𝒌(μ)−2​∑μ<νϕμ​(𝒌′)​ϕν​(𝒌′)​F𝒌​𝒌′(μ​ν).\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})F_{\bm{k}}^{(\mu)}-2\sum_{\mu<\nu}\phi_{\mu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\phi_{\nu}(\bm{k}^{\prime})F_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{(\mu\nu)}. (135)

where we define the form factors

F𝒌(μ)≡⟨Ψ2​M​|A𝒌†|​Ψ(μ)⟩,F𝒌​𝒌′(μ​ν)≡⟨Ψ2​M​|A𝒌†​A𝒌′†|​Ψ(μ​ν)⟩.F_{\bm{k}}^{(\mu)}\equiv\langle\Psi_{2M}\lvert A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\rvert\Psi^{(\mu)}\rangle,\qquad F_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{(\mu\nu)}\equiv\langle\Psi_{2M}\lvert A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rvert\Psi^{(\mu\nu)}\rangle. (136)

Define the general pair-creation operators

B†​(u)≡∑𝒑A𝒑†d𝒑−u,u∈ℂ.B^{\dagger}(u)\equiv\sum_{\bm{p}}\frac{A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}}{d_{\bm{p}}-u},\quad u\in\mathbb{C}. (137)

where d𝒑=2​ε𝒑d_{\bm{p}}=2\varepsilon_{\bm{p}}. For any choice of parameters {uμ}μ=1M\{u_{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{M}, this generates the general MM-pair state

|{u}⟩≡∏μ=1MB†​(uμ)​|0⟩.|\{u\}\rangle\equiv\prod_{\mu=1}^{M}B^{\dagger}(u_{\mu})\,|0\rangle. (138)

In particular, taking uμ=Eμu_{\mu}=E_{\mu} equal to the Richardson rapidities, we recover the Richardson state |Ψ2​M⟩=∏μ=1MB†​(Eμ)​|0⟩,B†​(Eμ)=∑𝒑=1A𝒑†d𝒑−Eμ,|\Psi_{2M}\rangle=\prod_{\mu=1}^{M}B^{\dagger}(E_{\mu})|0\rangle,\quad B^{\dagger}(E_{\mu})=\sum_{\bm{p}=1}\frac{A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}}{d_{\bm{p}}-E_{\mu}}, which matches the amplitudes ϕμ​(𝒑)=1/(d𝒑−Eμ)\phi_{\mu}(\bm{p})=1/(d_{\bm{p}}-E_{\mu}) we discussed. Now we can show the residue identity for A𝒌†A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}. From Eq. 137,

(d𝒌−u)​B†​(u)\displaystyle(d_{\bm{k}}-u)B^{\dagger}(u) =(d𝒌−u)​∑𝒑A𝒑†d𝒑−u=∑𝒑(d𝒌−u)​A𝒑†d𝒑−u\displaystyle=(d_{\bm{k}}-u)\sum_{\bm{p}}\frac{A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}}{d_{\bm{p}}-u}=\sum_{\bm{p}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)\frac{A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}}{d_{\bm{p}}-u} (139)

=12​∑𝒌d𝒌​N𝒌+g​∑𝒌,𝒌′A𝒌†​A𝒌′,(N𝒌≡n𝒌↑+n−𝒌↓).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{k}}d_{\bm{k}}N_{\bm{k}}+g\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}A_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}A_{\bm{k}^{\prime}},\quad(N_{\bm{k}}\equiv n_{\bm{k}\uparrow}+n_{-\bm{k}\downarrow}). (169)
