Eq. 167 and Eq. 172 are the final expressions of the pair-pair correlator, where d𝒌=2​ε𝒌d_{\bm{k}}=2\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}, matching the result from [43].

B.1.3 Slavnov’s Formula and Application

In this section, we will derive Eq. 146 and Eq. 147 used in Pair–Pair Correlators section (Sec. B.1.2). Recall the MM-pair states

|{u}⟩≡∏α=1MB†​(uα)​|0⟩,B†​(u)=∑𝒑A𝒑†d𝒑−u,|\{u\}\rangle\equiv\prod_{\alpha=1}^{M}B^{\dagger}(u_{\alpha})|0\rangle,\qquad B^{\dagger}(u)=\sum_{\bm{p}}\frac{A_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}}{d_{\bm{p}}-u}, (173)

and we defined the overlap

S({E},{F})≡⟨{E}|{F}|.⟩S(\{E\},\{F\})\equiv\left\langle\{E\}|\{F\}|.\right\rangle (174)

In this subsection, we assume {E}\{E\} is on-shell (namely, {E}\{E\} solves the Richardson equations), while {F}\{F\} is arbitrary and it does not need to solve the Richardson equations (we call it off-shell).

According to Slavnov’s formula and its application in Richardson model [132, 143, 29, 43], for on-shell {E}={E1,…,EM}\{E\}=\{E_{1},\dots,E_{M}\} and arbitrary {F}={F1,…,FM}\{F\}=\{F_{1},\dots,F_{M}\},

S⁡({E},{F})=∏b=1M∏a=1a≠bM(Ea−Fb)∏1≤a<b≤M(Eb−Ea)​∏1≤b<a≤M(Fb−Fa)​det𝒮⁡({E},{F}).S(\{E\},\{F\})=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{b=1}^{M}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}a=1\\ a\neq b\end{subarray}}^{M}\left(E_{a}-F_{b}\right)}{\displaystyle\prod_{1\leq a<b\leq M}\left(E_{b}-E_{a}\right)\prod_{1\leq b<a\leq M}\left(F_{b}-F_{a}\right)}\det\mathcal{S}(\{E\},\{F\}). (175)

and the M×MM\times M matrix 𝒮\mathcal{S} has entries (with a,b=1,…,Ma,b=1,...,M)

𝒮a​b​({E},{F})=Eb−FbEa−Fb​[∑i1(Ea−di)​(Fb−di)−2​∑c=1c≠aM1(Ea−Ec)​(Fb−Ec)].\mathcal{S}_{ab}(\{E\},\{F\})=\frac{E_{b}-F_{b}}{E_{a}-F_{b}}\left[\sum_{i}\frac{1}{(E_{a}-d_{i})(F_{b}-d_{i})}-2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c=1\\ c\neq a\end{subarray}}^{M}\frac{1}{(E_{a}-E_{c})(F_{b}-E_{c})}\right]. (176)

We now apply (175)–(176) to the specific sets in our case

{F(μ)​(u)}={E1,…,Eμ−1,u,Eμ+1,…,EM},{F(μ​ν)​(u,v)}={E1,…,u,…,v,…,EM},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\}=\{E_{1},\dots,E_{\mu-1},u,E_{\mu+1},\dots,E_{M}\},\qquad\{F^{(\mu\nu)}(u,v)\}=\{E_{1},\dots,u,\dots,v,\dots,E_{M}\}, (177)

because they are exactly the sets in our form factors (the factors to compute correlators) in Eq. 144 and Eq. 145:

F𝒌(μ)=limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​S​({E},{F(μ)​(u)}),F𝒌​𝒌′(μ​ν)=limu→d𝒌limv→d𝒌′(d𝒌−u)​(d𝒌′−v)​S​({E},{F(μ​ν)​(u,v)}).F_{\bm{k}}^{(\mu)}=\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)S(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\}),\qquad F_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{(\mu\nu)}=\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}\lim_{v\to d_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)(d_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}-v)S(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu\nu)}(u,v)\}). (178)

For {F}={F(μ)​(u)}\{F\}=\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\} we have Fb=EbF_{b}=E_{b} for b≠μb\neq\mu and Fμ=uF_{\mu}=u, so the prefactor in Eq. 175 can be reduced to 1:

∏b∏a≠b(Ea−Fb)∏a<b(Eb−Ea)​∏b<a(Fb−Fa)\displaystyle\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{b}\ \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\neq b\end{subarray}}(E_{a}-F_{b})}{\displaystyle\prod_{a<b}(E_{b}-E_{a})\;\prod_{b<a}(F_{b}-F_{a})} =∏b≠μ,a≠b(Ea−Eb)​∏a<b=μ(Ea−u)​∏a>b=μ(Ea−u)∏a<b(Eb−Ea)​∏b<ab,a≠μ(Eb−Ea)​∏b<a=μ(Eb−u)​∏a>b=μ(u−Ea)\displaystyle=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\neq\mu,a\neq b\end{subarray}}(E_{a}-E_{b})\prod_{a<b=\mu}(E_{a}-u)\prod_{a>b=\mu}(E_{a}-u)}{\displaystyle\prod_{a<b}(E_{b}-E_{a})\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}b<a\\ b,a\neq\mu\end{subarray}}(E_{b}-E_{a})\prod_{b<a=\mu}(E_{b}-u)\prod_{a>b=\mu}(u-E_{a})} (179)
=(∏b≠μ,a≠b(Ea−Eb)∏a<b(Eb−Ea)​∏b<ab,a≠μ(Eb−Ea))​(∏a<b=μ(Ea−u)∏b<a=μ(Eb−u))​(∏a>b=μ(Ea−u)∏a>b=μ(u−Ea))\displaystyle=(\frac{\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\neq\mu,a\neq b\end{subarray}}(E_{a}-E_{b})}{\prod_{a<b}(E_{b}-E_{a})\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}b<a\\ b,a\neq\mu\end{subarray}}(E_{b}-E_{a})})(\frac{\prod_{a<b=\mu}(E_{a}-u)}{\prod_{b<a=\mu}(E_{b}-u)})(\frac{\prod_{a>b=\mu}(E_{a}-u)}{\prod_{a>b=\mu}(u-E_{a})}) (180)
=(−1)M−μ​(1)​(−1)M−μ=(−1)2​(M−μ)=1.\displaystyle=(-1)^{M-\mu}(1)(-1)^{M-\mu}=(-1)^{2({M-\mu})}=1. (181)

Hence Eq. 175 becomes

S⁡({E},{F(μ)​(u)})=det𝒮⁡({E},{F(μ)​(u)}).S(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\})=\det\mathcal{S}\big(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\}\big). (182)

We now evaluate the limit Fb→EbF_{b}\to E_{b} in (176). First, for the columns b≠μb\neq\mu, according to Eq. 177, we have Fb=EbF_{b}=E_{b}, then

Off-diagonal (a≠ba\neq b):

limFb→Eb𝒮a​b\displaystyle\lim_{F_{b}\to E_{b}}\mathcal{S}_{ab} =limFb→EbEb−FbEa−Fb⋅−2(Ea−Eb)​(Fb−Eb)=−2(Ea−Eb)​limFb→EbEb−Fb(Ea−Fb)​(Fb−Eb)\displaystyle=\lim_{F_{b}\to E_{b}}\frac{E_{b}-F_{b}}{E_{a}-F_{b}}\cdot\frac{-2}{(E_{a}-E_{b})(F_{b}-E_{b})}=\frac{-2}{(E_{a}-E_{b})}\lim_{F_{b}\to E_{b}}\frac{E_{b}-F_{b}}{(E_{a}-F_{b})(F_{b}-E_{b})} (183)
=−2(Ea−Eb)​limFb→Eb−(Fb−Eb)(Ea−Fb)​(Fb−Eb)=2(Ea−Eb)​limFb→Eb1Ea−Fb=2(Ea−Eb)2.\displaystyle=\frac{-2}{(E_{a}-E_{b})}\,\lim_{F_{b}\to E_{b}}\frac{-(F_{b}-E_{b})}{(E_{a}-F_{b})(F_{b}-E_{b})}=\frac{2}{(E_{a}-E_{b})}\lim_{F_{b}\to E_{b}}\frac{1}{E_{a}-F_{b}}=\frac{2}{(E_{a}-E_{b})^{2}}. (184)

Diagonal (a=ba=b):

limFb→Eb𝒮b​b\displaystyle\lim_{F_{b}\to E_{b}}\mathcal{S}_{bb} =limFb→EbEb−FbEb−Fb​[∑i1(Eb−di)​(Fb−di)−2​∑c≠b1(Eb−Ec)​(Fb−Ec)]=∑i1(Eb−di)2−2​∑c≠b1(Eb−Ec)2.\displaystyle=\lim_{F_{b}\to E_{b}}\frac{E_{b}-F_{b}}{E_{b}-F_{b}}\left[\sum_{i}\frac{1}{(E_{b}-d_{i})(F_{b}-d_{i})}-2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\neq b\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{(E_{b}-E_{c})(F_{b}-E_{c})}\right]=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{(E_{b}-d_{i})^{2}}-2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\neq b\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{(E_{b}-E_{c})^{2}}. (185)

Comparing (184)–(185) with the Gaudin matrix GG in Eq. 116, we conclude: for every b≠μb\neq\mu, the bb-th column of 𝒮⁡({E},{F(μ)​(u)})\mathcal{S}(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\}) matches exactly the bb-th column of GG in the limit Fb→EbF_{b}\to E_{b}. Hence, inside the determinant (182), all columns except the μ\mu-th become Gaudin columns.

Second, for the special column b=μb=\mu, we have Fμ=uF_{\mu}=u. Multiply (176) by (d𝒌−u)(d_{\bm{k}}-u) and take u→d𝒌u\to d_{\bm{k}}. Only the 𝒊=𝒌\bm{i}=\bm{k} term in the first sum is singular, therefore,

limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​𝒮a​μ\displaystyle\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)\mathcal{S}_{a\mu} =limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​Eμ−uEa−u​1(Ea−d𝒌)​(u−d𝒌)=Eμ−d𝒌Ea−d𝒌​−1Ea−d𝒌=d𝒌−Eμ(d𝒌−Ea)2.\displaystyle=\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)\frac{E_{\mu}-u}{E_{a}-u}\frac{1}{(E_{a}-d_{\bm{k}})(u-d_{\bm{k}})}=\frac{E_{\mu}-d_{\bm{k}}}{E_{a}-d_{\bm{k}}}\frac{-1}{E_{a}-d_{\bm{k}}}=\frac{d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu}}{(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{a})^{2}}. (186)

Define the vector Ca(𝒌)≡1(d𝒌−Ea)2,C^{(\bm{k})}_{a}\equiv\frac{1}{(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{a})^{2}}, with a=1,…,M,a=1,\dots,M, then

limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​𝒮a​μ=(d𝒌−Eμ)​Ca(𝒌).\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)\mathcal{S}_{a\mu}=(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})C^{(\bm{k})}_{a}. (187)

Namely, as a column vector statement:

limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​𝒮μ​(u)=(d𝒌−Eμ)​C(𝒌),\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)\mathcal{S}_{\mu}(u)=(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})C^{(\bm{k})}, (188)

where C(𝒌)C^{(\bm{k})} is the column vector with components Ca(𝒌)C_{a}^{(\bm{k})}.

Multiply Eq. 182 by (d𝒌−u)(d_{\bm{k}}-u) and take the limit:

limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​S​({E},{F(μ)​(u)})=limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​det(𝒮⁡({E},{F(μ)​(u)})).\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)S\bigl(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\}\bigr)=\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)\det\Bigl(\mathcal{S}\bigl(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\}\bigr)\Bigr). (189)

Since only the μ\mu-th column of 𝒮⁡({E},{F(μ)​(u)})\mathcal{S}\bigl(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\}\bigr) contains a pole as we take the limit (having finite limit), multiplying its determinant by (d𝒌−u)(d_{\bm{k}}-u) and taking u→d𝒌u\to d_{\bm{k}} is equivalent to replacing the μ\mu-th column by (d𝒌−Eμ)​C(𝒌)(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})C^{(\bm{k})} (see Eq. 188), while all other columns become Gaudin matrix’s columns (see (184)–(185)). Thus,

limu→d𝒌(d𝒌−u)​S​({E},{F(μ)​(u)})=(d𝒌−Eμ)​detG⁡(μ→C(𝒌)),\lim_{u\to d_{\bm{k}}}(d_{\bm{k}}-u)S(\{E\},\{F^{(\mu)}(u)\})=(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})\det G\big(\mu\rightarrow C^{(\bm{k})}\big), (190)

where G⁡(μ→C(k))G(\mu\rightarrow C^{(k)}) denotes the matrix obtained from GG by replacing its μ\mu-th column with C(𝒌)C^{(\bm{k})}. Using Eq. 144 gives precisely Eq. 146 that we used in the previous subsection:

F𝒌(μ)=(d𝒌−Eμ)​det(G⁡(μ→C(𝒌))),F_{\bm{k}}^{(\mu)}=(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})\det\bigl(G(\mu\rightarrow C^{(\bm{k})})\bigr), (191)

Similarly, we can also show that

F𝒌​𝒌′(μ​ν)=(d𝒌−Eμ)​(d𝒌−Eν)​(d𝒌′−Eμ)​(d𝒌′−Eν)(d𝒌−d𝒌′)​(Eν−Eμ)det(G(μ,ν→C(𝒌),C(𝒌′))),(𝒌≠𝒌′)F_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{(\mu\nu)}=\frac{(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu})(d_{\bm{k}}-E_{\nu})(d_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}-E_{\mu})(d_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}-E_{\nu})}{(d_{\bm{k}}-d_{\bm{k}^{\prime}})(E_{\nu}-E_{\mu})}\,\det\bigl(G(\mu,\nu\rightarrow C^{(\bm{k})},C^{(\bm{k}^{\prime})})\bigr),\quad(\bm{k}\neq\bm{k}^{\prime}) (192)

as claimed in Eq. 147, where G(μ,ν→C(𝒌),C(𝒌′))G(\mu,\nu\rightarrow C^{(\bm{k})},C^{(\bm{k}^{\prime})}) denotes the matrix obtained from GG by replacing the μ\mu-th and ν\nu-th columns by C(𝒌)C^{(\bm{k})} and C(𝒌′)C^{(\bm{k}^{\prime})}, respectively.

B.1.4 Numerical Exact Pair-Pair Correlator Data

We solve the Richardson equations Eq. 111 on 2-dimensional Richardson models  [115, 114, 26] on L=6,12,18L=6,12,18 respectively, with fixed electron filling 2​M/L22M/L^{2} = 1/6. On each L×LL\times L BZ mesh we sample

𝒌=(kx,ky),kx=2​πLnx,ky=2​πLny,nx,ny∈{0,1,…,L−1},\bm{k}=(k_{x},k_{y}),\qquad k_{x}=\frac{2\pi}{L}\,n_{x},\quad k_{y}=\frac{2\pi}{L}\,n_{y},\qquad n_{x},n_{y}\in\{0,1,\ldots,L-1\}, (193)

with single–particle energy

ε𝒌=t⁡(cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky).\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}=t(\cos k_{x}+\cos k_{y}). (194)

We choose hopping t=0.1t=0.1 in this work. For each of the meshes, we calculate the numerical pair-pair correlator data using Eq. 167 and Eq. 172.

B.1.5 Exact-Diagonalization (ED) Validation

We validate our numerical Richardson-equation solver by benchmarking against ED calculation on small system sizes in the fully-paired sector. For each L×LL\times L momentum grid and coupling g=u/L2g=u/L^{2} with u=−1u=-1, we solve the Richardson equations for the rapidities {Eμ}μ=1M\{E_{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{M} and compute the many-body energy Enumerical=∑μ=1MEμE_{\mathrm{numerical}}=\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}E_{\mu}. For the cases L=2L=2, Ne=2N_{e}=2 and L=4L=4, Ne=4N_{e}=4, our EnumericalE_{\mathrm{numerical}} matches the ED ground-state energy exactly (with differences at most ∼10−16\sim 10^{-16}), and the 1g+∑𝒌12​ε𝒌−Eμ−∑ν≠μ2Eν−Eμ\frac{1}{g}+\sum_{\bm{k}}\frac{1}{2\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-E_{\mu}}-\sum_{\nu\neq\mu}\frac{2}{E_{\nu}-E_{\mu}} are negligible (∼10−16\sim 10^{-16} and ∼10−14\sim 10^{-14} respectively), confirming that our solver converges to the exact solution.

We also further validate our pair–pair correlator evaluation by benchmarking against ED. Using the same momentum grid, electron filling, u, and g, we compute the correlator matrix in two independent ways: (i) from the Richardson rapidities {Eμ}\{E_{\mu}\} via the closed-form expressions, Eq. 167 and Eq. 172, and (ii) directly from the ED ground-state wavefunction in the MM-pair Hilbert space. For the small-size test cases (e.g., L=2,Ne=2L=2,N_{e}=2 and L=4,Ne=4L=4,N_{e}=4), the resulting C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} agree exactly, confirming the correctness of our numerical correlator solver.

B.2 ML Results

We wish to train a NN on the pair-pair correlation function (a special 22-RDM) C∈ℝL2×L2C\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times L^{2}}, which is a symmetric positive semi-definite real matrix with L4L^{4} elements in total. Since the self-attention mechanism has quadratic time and space complexity, the memory requirements are proportional to L8L^{8}, which can be extremely difficult for large LL. Therefore, we chose to focus exclusively on the SIREN architecture for this model.

Numerically, the eigenvalue spectrum of CC is dominated by a single eigenvalue, with the remaining eigenvalues suppressed by several orders of magnitude. Consequently, the matrix has an effective rank close to 1. As such, we can diagonalize CC for each value of LL and choose 𝑨∈ℝL2×1\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times 1} to be a normalized (i.e., ‖𝑨‖2=1||\bm{A}||_{2}=1) eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. Since the trace of the correlator is equal to L212\frac{L^{2}}{12} (electron pair number), CC can then be approximately reconstructed as C≈L212​𝑨​𝑨TC\approx\frac{L^{2}}{12}\bm{A}\bm{A}^{T}.

Note that we can reshape 𝑨\bm{A} into a matrix of shape L×LL\times L, which matches the matrix dimensions in the 1-RDM case. Thus, we train a SIREN to output the elements of 𝑨\bm{A} given 2D normalized coordinates, as described in Sec. A.2. For inference, we enforce full D4D_{4} symmetry by averaging the SIREN predictions for large LL with all of their rotations and reflections (i.e. the entire group of symmetries of the square). However, during training, we instead allow the SIREN to learn the symmetry by adding another term to the loss function in Eq. 61:

ℒsymmetry=λsymmetry​(1|S|)​∑g∈SMSE​(𝑨~,g⁡(𝑨~)),\mathcal{L}_{\text{symmetry}}=\lambda_{\text{symmetry}}\left(\frac{1}{|S|}\right)\sum_{g\in S}\text{MSE}\left(\widetilde{\bm{A}},g(\widetilde{\bm{A}})\right), (195)

where 𝑨~∈ℝ(L+1)×(L+1)\widetilde{\bm{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(L+1)\times(L+1)} is the “wrapped around” version of the reshaped 𝑨\bm{A} matrix for large L (see Sec. A.2.2 for details), SS is a generating subset of D4D_{4} (​i.e.,D4=⟨S⟩{\emph{i.e.}},D_{4}=\langle S\rangle), which we choose to be S={R90,D}S=\{R_{90},D\} (R90R_{90} denotes rotation by 90∘90^{\circ} and DD denotes a reflection across the main diagonal), |S||S| is the cardinality of SS (|S|=2|S|=2 in our case), and the λsymmetry\lambda_{\text{symmetry}} coefficient (a hyperparameter) controls the contribution to the total loss function. This symmetry loss is added after a small number of warmup steps (5050 steps in our case) to prevent gradients from misleading the training by chasing a moving target. For training on the Richardson model, we omit the optional statistical prior (TV/FH) described in the general SIREN architecture (see Sec. A.2.5 for details), so we choose 𝒫=0\mathcal{P}=0 in Eq. 61. Finally, we use the Tree-Structured Parzen Estimation (TPE) [6] algorithm to search for the optimal hyperparameter configuration that can enable the SIREN to generalize effectively to larger LL, as intended. For each trial, the SIREN is allowed to be trained for a total of 500500 epochs, although we also save intermediate checkpoints in order to find the optimal parameter values.

Using the above method, we trained a SIREN on 𝑨\bm{A} for L=6L=6, and then used it to predict 𝑨\bm{A} for L=12L=12 and L=18L=18. For each test size, 𝑨\bm{A} is first normalized such that ‖𝑨‖2=1||\bm{A}||_{2}=1 (where ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} denotes the ℓ2\ell^{2} norm) before reconstructing the predicted final 22-RDM via:

CSIREN=L212​𝑨​𝑨T.C^{\text{SIREN}}=\frac{L^{2}}{12}\bm{A}\bm{A}^{T}. (196)

For the Richardson model, the MSE is defined as:

MSE​(C,CSIREN)=1L4​∑i=1L2∑j=1L2(Ci​jSIREN−Ci​j)2,\text{MSE}(C,\,C^{\text{SIREN}})=\frac{1}{L^{4}}\sum_{i=1}^{L^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{L^{2}}\left(C^{\text{SIREN}}_{ij}-C_{ij}\right)^{2}, (197)

where CSIRENC^{\text{SIREN}} and CC are the SIREN-predicted final values and the true final values for the 22-RDM of pair-pair correlators, respectively. In order to evaluate the trained SIREN’s performance, we take the square root of Eq. 197, ​i.e.MSE{\emph{i.e.}}\ \sqrt{\text{MSE}}, in order to ensure that the power on the unit of the error is the same as that for CC and CSIRENC^{\text{SIREN}}. To measure the relative accuracy rnr_{n}, we normalize the MSE\sqrt{\text{MSE}} by the total range of values of the original CC, and subtract this fraction from unity. Results are shown in Tab. 2. We can also compare the predicted final 22-RDM from the SIREN to the true final 22-RDM (i.e. the actual values of CC) visually, as shown in Fig. 9 for a test size of L=12L=12. (See Fig. 4 in the maintext for a comparison on L=18L=18.)

Next, we train an additional SIREN on 4 L1×L2L_{1}\times L_{2} tilted meshes with different side lengths L1,L2∈ℤ>0L_{1},L_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. Define 𝒃1=(2​π,0)\bm{b}_{1}=(2\pi,0) and 𝒃2=(0,2​π)\bm{b}_{2}=(0,2\pi) to be the primitive reciprocal lattice vectors. For each tilted mesh, we construct the transformed reciprocal lattice vectors 𝒇1\bm{f}_{1} and 𝒇2\bm{f}_{2} as a linear combination of 𝒃1\bm{b}_{1} and 𝒃2\bm{b}_{2}, ​i.e.{\emph{i.e.}} (𝒇1,𝒇2)T=M​(𝒃1,𝒃2)T\left(\bm{f}_{1},\bm{f}_{2}\right)^{T}=M\left(\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2}\right)^{T}, where M∈ℤ2×2M\in\mathbb{Z}^{2\times 2} is different for each tilted mesh. The side lengths and transformed reciprocal lattice vectors are chosen so that each tilted mesh has L1​L2=12L_{1}L_{2}=12 𝒌\bm{k} points, and so that the overlap between different meshes (​i.e.{\emph{i.e.}}, the number of 𝒌\bm{k} points in common) is minimized as shown in Fig. 10. We diagonalize C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} for each tilted mesh, and choose the normalized eigenvector 𝑨∈ℝL1​L2\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{1}L_{2}} corresponding to the highest eigenvalue, which can be viewed as a function of L1​L2L_{1}L_{2} 𝒌\bm{k} points. By combining the eigenvectors for all four of the tilted meshes, we obtain the training dataset for the SIREN after normalizing the 𝒌\bm{k} points to lie in [−1,1]2[-1,1]^{2} and enforcing periodic boundary conditions for each reshaped eigenvector (see Sec. A.2.2). We train for a total of 10001000 epochs, and apply the D4D_{4} symmetry loss according to Eq. 195 after the first 2020 epochs. Note that we do not use TPE [6] to optimize hyperparameters, as was done when training on L=6L=6. After training, the resulting SIREN is then used to predict a new eigenvector, which we divide by its ℓ2\ell^{2} norm to produce 𝑨∈ℝ182\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{18^{2}} for L=18L=18, where ‖𝑨‖=1||\bm{A}||=1. The corresponding C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} is again reconstructed via Eq. 196, after which we compute the accuracy with respect to the true final C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} using Eq. 197. The result yields a relative accuracy of rn=93.77%r_{n}=93.77\%. A comparison between CSIRENC^{\text{SIREN}} and the true C𝒌​𝒌′C_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}} for this case can be seen in Fig. 11.

Appendix C Translation-invariant 1-RDM in a four-band model

C.1 Model Set-Up

We work on an L×LL\times L Bravis lattice with a four-component orbital (or layer/sublattice) spinor ψ𝒓=(ψ𝒓,1,…,ψ𝒓,4)𝖳\psi_{\bm{r}}=(\psi_{\bm{r},1},\dots,\psi_{\bm{r},4})^{\mathsf{T}} at site 𝒓∈ℤ2\bm{r}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}. The real-space single-particle Hamiltonian contains on-site and short-range hoppings written with 4×44\times 4 matrices h⁡(𝜹)h(\bm{\delta}) that connect 𝒓\bm{r} to 𝒓+𝜹\bm{r}+\bm{\delta}:

H0=∑𝒓ψ𝒓†​h​(𝟎)​ψ𝒓+∑𝒓∑𝜹≠𝟎(ψ𝒓+𝜹†​h​(𝜹)​ψ𝒓+h.c.).H_{0}=\sum_{\bm{r}}\psi_{\bm{r}}^{\dagger}\,h(\bm{0})\,\psi_{\bm{r}}+\sum_{\bm{r}}\sum_{\bm{\delta}\neq\bm{0}}\Big(\psi_{\bm{r}+\bm{\delta}}^{\dagger}\,h(\bm{\delta})\,\psi_{\bm{r}}+\text{h.c.}\Big). (198)

We choose the five gamma matrices as

Γ1=σx⊗σx,Γ2=σx⊗σy,Γ3=σx⊗σz,Γ4=σy⊗𝕀,Γ5=σz⊗𝕀,\Gamma_{1}=\sigma_{x}\otimes\sigma_{x},\quad\Gamma_{2}=\sigma_{x}\otimes\sigma_{y},\quad\Gamma_{3}=\sigma_{x}\otimes\sigma_{z},\quad\Gamma_{4}=\sigma_{y}\otimes\mathbb{I},\quad\Gamma_{5}=\sigma_{z}\otimes\mathbb{I}, (199)

where σx\sigma_{x}, σy\sigma_{y} and σz\sigma_{z} are Pauli matrices. The hoppings have the following form:

on-site:\displaystyle\text{on-site:} h⁡(𝟎)=Γ5,\displaystyle h(\bm{0})=\Gamma_{5}, (200)
NN (odd, along x,y):\displaystyle\text{NN (odd, along $x,y$):} h(+𝒙^)=12​iΓ1,h(−𝒙^)=−12​iΓ1,h(+𝒚^)=12​iΓ2,h(−𝒚^)=−12​iΓ2,\displaystyle h(+\hat{\bm{x}})=\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{1},\quad h(-\hat{\bm{x}})=-\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{1},\qquad h(+\hat{\bm{y}})=\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{2},\quad h(-\hat{\bm{y}})=-\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{2},
NNN(odd, along x,y):\displaystyle\text{NNN(odd, along $x,y$):} h(+2𝒙^)=12​iΓ3,h(−2𝒙^)=−12​iΓ3,h(+2𝒚^)=12​iΓ4,h(−2𝒚^)=−12​iΓ4,\displaystyle h(+2\hat{\bm{x}})=\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{3},\quad h(-2\hat{\bm{x}})=-\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{3},\qquad h(+2\hat{\bm{y}})=\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{4},\quad h(-2\hat{\bm{y}})=-\tfrac{1}{2i}\Gamma_{4},
NN (even, in the Γ5 channel):\displaystyle\text{NN (even, in the $\Gamma_{5}$ channel):} h(±𝒙^)=12Γ5,h(±𝒚^)=12Γ5.\displaystyle h(\pm\hat{\bm{x}})=\tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma_{5},\qquad h(\pm\hat{\bm{y}})=\tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma_{5}.

Here “NN” denotes nearest–neighbor displacements 𝜹\bm{\delta} with |𝜹|=1|\bm{\delta}|=1 (±𝒙^,±𝒚^\pm\hat{\bm{x}},\,\pm\hat{\bm{y}}); “NNN” denotes next–nearest neighbors along the axes |𝜹|=2|\bm{\delta}|=2 (±2​𝒙^,±2​𝒚^\pm 2\hat{\bm{x}},\,\pm 2\hat{\bm{y}}). Unlisted h⁡(𝜹)h(\bm{\delta}) are zero. With the lattice Fourier transform

ψ𝒓=1L2∑𝒌ei​𝒌⋅rψ𝒌,𝒌=(kx,ky)∈[0,2π)2,\psi_{\bm{r}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L^{2}}}\sum_{\bm{k}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot r}\,\psi_{\bm{k}},\qquad\bm{k}=(k_{x},k_{y})\in[0,2\pi)^{2}, (201)

Eq. 198 becomes

H0\displaystyle H_{0} =∑𝒓ψ𝒓†​h​(𝟎)​ψ𝒓+∑𝒓∑𝜹≠𝟎(ψ𝒓+𝜹†​h​(𝜹)​ψ𝒓+h.c.)\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{r}}\psi_{\bm{r}}^{\dagger}h(\bm{0})\psi_{\bm{r}}+\sum_{\bm{r}}\sum_{\bm{\delta}\neq\bm{0}}\big(\psi_{\bm{r}+\bm{\delta}}^{\dagger}h(\bm{\delta})\psi_{\bm{r}}+\text{h.c.}\big) (202)
=1L2∑𝒓∑𝒌,𝒌′e−i𝒌′⋅𝒓ψ𝒌′†h(𝟎)ei​𝒌⋅𝒓ψ𝒌+1L2∑𝒓∑𝜹≠𝟎∑𝒌,𝒌′e−i𝒌′⋅(𝒓+𝜹)ψ𝒌′†h(𝜹)ei​𝒌⋅𝒓ψ𝒌+h.c.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{r}}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}e^{-i\bm{k}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{r}}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\,h(\bm{0})\,e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}\psi_{\bm{k}}+\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{r}}\sum_{\bm{\delta}\neq\bm{0}}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}e^{-i\bm{k}^{\prime}\cdot(\bm{r}+\bm{\delta})}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\,h(\bm{\delta})\,e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}\psi_{\bm{k}}+\text{h.c.}
=∑𝒌,𝒌′ψ𝒌′†h(𝟎)ψ𝒌1L2∑𝒓ei⁡(𝒌−𝒌′)⋅𝒓+∑𝜹≠𝟎∑𝒌,𝒌′ψ𝒌′†h(𝜹)ψ𝒌1L2∑𝒓ei⁡(𝒌−𝒌′)⋅𝒓e−i𝒌′⋅𝜹+h.c.\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\,h(\bm{0})\,\psi_{\bm{k}}\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{r}}e^{i(\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\cdot\bm{r}}+\sum_{\bm{\delta}\neq\bm{0}}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\,h(\bm{\delta})\,\psi_{\bm{k}}\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{r}}e^{i(\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\cdot\bm{r}}\,e^{-i\bm{k}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{\delta}}+\text{h.c.}
=∑𝒌ψ𝒌†h(𝟎)ψ𝒌+∑𝜹≠𝟎∑𝒌ψ𝒌†(ei​𝒌⋅𝜹h(𝜹))ψ𝒌+h.c.(1L2∑𝒓ei⁡(𝒌−𝒌′)⋅𝒓=δ𝒌,𝒌′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}}\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}h(\bm{0})\psi_{\bm{k}}+\sum_{\bm{\delta}\neq\bm{0}}\sum_{\bm{k}}\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\big(e^{\,i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}}h(\bm{\delta})\big)\psi_{\bm{k}}+\text{h.c.}\qquad\bigg(\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{r}}e^{i(\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\cdot\bm{r}}=\delta_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\bigg)
=∑𝒌ψ𝒌†[h(𝟎)+∑𝜹≠𝟎(ei​𝒌⋅𝜹h(𝜹)+e−i𝒌⋅𝜹h†(𝜹))]ψ𝒌\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}}\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\Big[h(\bm{0})+\sum_{\bm{\delta}\neq\bm{0}}\big(e^{\,i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}}h(\bm{\delta})+e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}}h^{\dagger}(\bm{\delta})\big)\Big]\psi_{\bm{k}}
≡∑𝒌ψ𝒌†H0(𝒌)ψ𝒌,H0(𝒌)=h(𝟎)+∑𝜹≠𝟎(ei​𝒌⋅𝜹h(𝜹)+e−i𝒌⋅𝜹h†(𝜹))=∑a=15da(𝒌)Γa,\displaystyle\equiv\sum_{\bm{k}}\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}H_{0}(\bm{k})\psi_{\bm{k}},\qquad H_{0}(\bm{k})=h(\bm{0})+\sum_{\bm{\delta}\neq\bm{0}}\big(e^{\,i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}}h(\bm{\delta})+e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}}h^{\dagger}(\bm{\delta})\big)=\sum_{a=1}^{5}d_{a}(\bm{k})\Gamma_{a},

and the form factors are

d1=sin⁡kx,d2=sin⁡ky,d3=sin⁡(2​kx),d4=sin⁡(2​ky),d5=1+cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky.d_{1}=\sin k_{x},\quad d_{2}=\sin k_{y},\quad d_{3}=\sin(2k_{x}),\quad d_{4}=\sin(2k_{y}),\quad d_{5}=1+\cos k_{x}+\cos k_{y}. (203)

The odd/even harmonics follow from e±i𝒌⋅𝜹=(cos𝒌⋅𝜹)±i(sin𝒌⋅𝜹)e^{\pm i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}}=(\cos\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta})\pm i(\sin\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}): antisymmetric pairs h⁡(+δ)=−h⁡(−δ)h(+\delta)=-h(-\delta) generate sin\sin, while symmetric pairs h⁡(+𝜹)=h⁡(−𝜹)h(+\bm{\delta})=h(-\bm{\delta}) generate cos\cos. By the Clifford algebra of the Γa\Gamma_{a}, the spectrum is doubly degenerate with

E±​(𝒌)=±‖d⁡(𝒌)‖=±∑a=15da​(𝒌)2.E_{\pm}(\bm{k})=\pm\|d(\bm{k})\|=\pm\sqrt{\sum_{a=1}^{5}d_{a}(\bm{k})^{2}}. (204)

At filling f=1f=1 we occupy the lower band. We diagnose its topology via the Wilson loop Wx​(ky)W_{x}(k_{y}) of the occupied projector P⁡(𝒌)P(\bm{k}) in Eq. 210, yielding the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} index νℤ2=1\nu_{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}=1. This certifies that our training/benchmark data come from a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} non-trivial phase. For the interaction in second quantization and its lattice Fourier transform Eq. 63,

Hint\displaystyle H_{\text{int}} =12​∑𝒓∑𝑹V⁡(𝑹)​n𝒓​n𝒓+𝑹\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{r}}\sum_{\bm{R}}V(\bm{R})\,n_{\bm{r}}\,n_{\bm{r}+\bm{R}}
=12∑𝒓,𝑹V(𝑹)(1N∑𝒌ei​𝒌⋅𝒓ψ𝒌†)(1N∑𝒌′e−i𝒌′⋅𝒓ψ𝒌′)(1N∑𝒑ei​𝒑⋅(𝒓+𝑹)ψ𝒑†)(1N∑𝒑′e−i𝒑′⋅(𝒓+𝑹)ψ𝒑′)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{r},\bm{R}}V(\bm{R})\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{k}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}\,\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}e^{-i\bm{k}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{r}}\,\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{p}}e^{i\bm{p}\cdot(\bm{r}+\bm{R})}\,\psi_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{p}^{\prime}}e^{-i\bm{p}^{\prime}\cdot(\bm{r}+\bm{R})}\,\psi_{\bm{p}^{\prime}}\right)
=12​N2​∑𝑹V⁡(𝑹)​∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒑,𝒑′(∑𝒓ei⁡(𝒌−𝒌′+𝒑−𝒑′)⋅𝒓)​ei⁡(𝒑−𝒑′)⋅𝑹​ψ𝒌†​ψ𝒌′​ψ𝒑†​ψ𝒑′\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N^{2}}\sum_{\bm{R}}V(\bm{R})\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{p},\bm{p}^{\prime}}\Big(\sum_{\bm{r}}e^{i(\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{p}-\bm{p}^{\prime})\cdot\bm{r}}\Big)e^{i(\bm{p}-\bm{p}^{\prime})\cdot\bm{R}}\,\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\psi_{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{p}^{\prime}}
=12​N∑𝑹V(𝑹)∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒒e−i𝒒⋅𝑹ψ𝒌+𝒒†ψ𝒌ψ𝒌′−𝒒†ψ𝒌′(𝒒≡𝒑′−𝒑)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\bm{R}}V(\bm{R})\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{q}}e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}\,\psi_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k}}\,\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{q}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}\qquad(\bm{q}\equiv\bm{p}^{\prime}-\bm{p})
=12​N​∑𝒒(∑𝑹V(𝑹)e−i𝒒⋅𝑹)⏟U⁡(𝒒)​∑𝒌,𝒌′ψ𝒌+𝒒†​ψ𝒌​ψ𝒌′−𝒒†​ψ𝒌′.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\bm{q}}\underbrace{\Big(\sum_{\bm{R}}V(\bm{R})e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}\Big)}_{U(\bm{q})}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\psi_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k}}\,\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{q}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}. (205)

Thus the translation-invariant interaction enters through the lattice Fourier transform,

U(𝒒)=∑𝑹V(𝑹)e−i𝒒⋅𝑹.U(\bm{q})=\sum_{\bm{R}}V(\bm{R})\,e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}. (206)

For our specific short-range choice

V⁡(𝑹)=U0​[δ𝑹,𝟎+12​(δ𝑹,𝒙^+δ𝑹,−𝒙^+δ𝑹,𝒚^+δ𝑹,−𝒚^)]V(\bm{R})=U_{0}\left[\delta_{\bm{R},\bm{0}}+\frac{1}{2}\big(\delta_{\bm{R},\hat{\bm{x}}}+\delta_{\bm{R},-\hat{\bm{x}}}+\delta_{\bm{R},\hat{\bm{y}}}+\delta_{\bm{R},-\hat{\bm{y}}}\big)\right] (207)

Therefore,

U(𝒒)=∑𝑹V(𝑹)e−i𝒒⋅𝑹=U0[1+12(e−i​qx+e+i​qx+e−i​qy+e+i​qy)]=U0(1+cosqx+cosqy).U(\bm{q})=\sum_{\bm{R}}V(\bm{R})e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}=U_{0}\left[1+\tfrac{1}{2}\big(e^{-iq_{x}}+e^{+iq_{x}}+e^{-iq_{y}}+e^{+iq_{y}}\big)\right]=U_{0}\big(1+\cos q_{x}+\cos q_{y}\big). (208)

So the momentum-space interaction is

Hint=12​N​∑𝒒U0​(1+cos⁡qx+cos⁡qy)​∑𝒌,𝒌′ψ𝒌+𝒒†​ψ𝒌​ψ𝒌′−𝒒†​ψ𝒌′.H_{\text{int}}=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\bm{q}}U_{0}\big(1+\cos q_{x}+\cos q_{y}\big)\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime}}\psi_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k}}\,\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{q}}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k}^{\prime}}. (209)

The mean-field order parameter is the 1-RDM (projector onto occupied HF bands) at each momentum:

P⁡(𝒌)=∑n=1f|un​(𝒌)⟩​⟨un​(𝒌)|,P(\bm{k})=\sum_{n=1}^{f}\,|u_{n}(\bm{k})\rangle\langle u_{n}(\bm{k})|, (210)

where n is the band index, and f∈{1,2,3,4}f\in\{1,2,3,4\} is the filling (number of occupied bands per 𝒌\bm{k}). We choose f=1f=1 for our ML training. The projector obeys

P†​(𝒌)=P⁡(𝒌),P2​(𝒌)=P⁡(𝒌),tr⁡P⁡(𝒌)=f.P^{\dagger}(\bm{k})=P(\bm{k}),\qquad P^{2}(\bm{k})=P(\bm{k}),\qquad\operatorname{tr}P(\bm{k})=f. (211)

Normal ordering the interaction with respect to P⁡(𝒌)P(\bm{k}) yields the self-consistent HF Hamiltonian

HHF​(𝒌)=H0​(𝒌)+ΣH+ΣF​(𝒌,[P]),H_{\mathrm{HF}}(\bm{k})=H_{0}(\bm{k})+\Sigma_{H}+\Sigma_{F}(\bm{k};[P]), (212)

with a Hartree shift

ΣH=U⁡(0)​n¯​𝕀4,n¯≡1L2​∑𝒌tr⁡P⁡(𝒌),\Sigma_{H}=U(0)\,\bar{n}\mathbb{I}_{4},\quad\bar{n}\equiv\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{k}}\operatorname{tr}P(\bm{k}), (213)

and a Fock self-energy given by a BZ convolution

ΣF(𝒌;[P])=−1L2∑𝒒U(𝒒)P(𝒌+𝒒).\Sigma_{F}(\bm{k};[P])=-\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{q}}U(\bm{q})\,P(\bm{k}+\bm{q}). (214)

Because ΣH∝𝕀4\Sigma_{H}\propto\mathbb{I}_{4} and tr⁡P⁡(𝒌)=f\operatorname{tr}P(\bm{k})=f is fixed by the filling, the Hartree term produces a uniform band shift and does not affect the projector; symmetry breaking (if any) is controlled by ΣF\Sigma_{F}. We monitor the total energy density (per unit cell)

ℰ⁡[P]=12​L2​∑𝒌tr⁡[(HHF​(𝒌)+H0​(𝒌))​P​(𝒌)],\mathcal{E}[P]=\frac{1}{2L^{2}}\sum_{\bm{k}}\operatorname{tr}\Bigl[\bigl(H_{\mathrm{HF}}(\bm{k})+H_{0}(\bm{k})\bigr)\,P(\bm{k})\Bigr], (215)

where the factor 1/21/2 avoids double counting. The stopping criterion is |ℰn+1−ℰn|<10−6\big|\mathcal{E}_{n+1}-\mathcal{E}_{n}\big|<10^{-6}, supplemented by the mean-squared change of the projector between iterations. Arrays H0​(𝒌)H_{0}(\bm{k}), U⁡(𝒒)U(\bm{q}), and P⁡(𝒌)P(\bm{k}) live on the BZ grid. Given P(n)P^{(n)}, we build ΣH​[P(n)]\Sigma_{H}[P^{(n)}] and ΣF​[P(n)]\Sigma_{F}[P^{(n)}], diagonalize HHF​[P(n)]​(𝒌)H_{\mathrm{HF}}[P^{(n)}](\bm{k}) at each 𝒌\bm{k}, and update

P(n+1)​(𝒌)=∑m=1f|um(n)​(𝒌)⟩​⟨um(n)​(𝒌)|,P^{(n+1)}(\bm{k})=\sum_{m=1}^{f}\,|u^{(n)}_{m}(\bm{k})\rangle\langle u^{(n)}_{m}(\bm{k})|, (216)

selecting the ff eigenvectors with the lowest eigenvalues (ordered by real part).

The four-band model supplies the final HF labels — P⁡(𝒌)P(\bm{k}) at filling f=1f=1 and band energies ℰ\mathcal{E} — from a translation-invariant HF calculation, by which we pretrain and validate our NN architectures. It provides a clean benchmark to quantify acceleration: we compare HF iteration counts when initialized with the NN-predicted final 1-RDM versus a random initial 1-RDM at a fixed tolerance.

C.2 ML Results

Translation-invariant systems are simpler because the one-body correlator is diagonal in momentum (𝒌=𝒌′\bm{k}=\bm{k}^{\prime}), so inference reduces to a sequence of L2L^{2} matrices. The lower dimensionality lets us use a conventional self-attention NN without neural representation (SIREN). We again work on the discrete BZ with 𝒌\bm{k} in Eq. (4). Index grid points by their integers (l1,l2)(l_{1},l_{2}) with l1,2∈{0,…,L−1}l_{1,2}\in\{0,\dots,L-1\}, so that

𝒌⁡(l1,l2)=l1L​𝒃1+l2L​𝒃2.\bm{k}(l_{1},l_{2})=\frac{l_{1}}{L}\,\bm{b}_{1}+\frac{l_{2}}{L}\,\bm{b}_{2}.

To encode relative position with periodic boundary conditions, use the wrapped (minimum-image) index differences

Δ​l1=((l1−l1′+⌊L/2⌋)modL)−⌊L/2⌋,Δ​l2=((l2−l2′+⌊L/2⌋)modL)−⌊L/2⌋,\Delta l_{1}=\big((l_{1}-l_{1}^{\prime}+\lfloor L/2\rfloor)\bmod L\big)-\lfloor L/2\rfloor,\quad\Delta l_{2}=\big((l_{2}-l_{2}^{\prime}+\lfloor L/2\rfloor)\bmod L\big)-\lfloor L/2\rfloor, (217)

so we can define the 2D coordinate

𝒙(l1,l2),(l1′,l2′)=(Δ​l1L,Δ​l2L).\bm{x}_{(l_{1},l_{2}),(l_{1}^{\prime},l_{2}^{\prime})}=\Big(\tfrac{\Delta l_{1}}{L},\,\tfrac{\Delta l_{2}}{L}\Big). (218)

For brevity we denote 𝒙(l1,l2),(l1′,l2′)\bm{x}_{(l_{1},l_{2}),(l_{1}^{\prime},l_{2}^{\prime})} as 𝒙i​j\bm{x}_{ij}.

For the four-band model we keep the architecture of Sec. A.1 but, given the simplicity here, replace the custom Fourier-based bias by a small MLP, following the formulation of Ref. [74]. That is,

Bi​j=fθ​(𝒌i,𝒌j)=GELU⁡(𝒙i​j​W1+𝒃1)​W2+b2.B_{ij}=f_{\theta}\big(\bm{k}_{i},\bm{k}_{j}\big)=\mathrm{GELU}\big(\bm{x}_{ij}W_{1}+\bm{b}_{1}\big)\,W_{2}+b_{2}. (219)

where 𝒙i​j\bm{x}_{ij} represents the relative coordinate between two kk-points in 2D momentum space and W1∈ℳ2×dMLP​(ℝ)W_{1}\in\mathcal{M}_{2\times d_{\mathrm{MLP}}}(\mathbb{R}), 𝒃1∈ℝdMLP\bm{b}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{MLP}}}, W2∈ℳdMLP×1​(ℝ)W_{2}\in\mathcal{M}_{d_{\mathrm{MLP}}\times 1}(\mathbb{R}), 𝒃2∈ℝ\bm{b}_{2}\in\mathbb{R} are all filled with learnable parameters to be optimized during training, and dMLPd_{\mathrm{MLP}} represents the size of the hidden layer in the MLP. Eq. 219 replaces Eq. 29 for the bias function in the four-band model. Thus, the output of fθf_{\theta} is a scalar bias (that quantifies how closely related the corresponding 𝒌\bm{k} points are), which is then added to the self-attention computation via Eq. 32, thereby injecting relative positional information into the NN.

C.2.1 Hyperparameters

To train the self-attention NN, we used a constant learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. A full list of the hyperparameters used can be seen in Tab. 3.

C.2.2 Standardization

For the translation-invariant case, given O𝒌,α​α′𝒒=0O_{\bm{k},\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}^{\bm{q}=0} we construct XinitX_{\mathrm{init}} and XtgtX_{\mathrm{tgt}} as in Eq. 13 and Eq. 7. To standardize the data, we compute the mean and standard deviations across all features f∈{1,…​2​ξ2}f\in\{1,\dots 2\xi^{2}\}. That is, for all NsampleN_{\text{sample}} training samples with β∈{init,tgt}\beta\in\{\text{init},\text{tgt}\}:

μf(β)≡1Nsample​L2​(2​ξ2)​∑sample∑i=1L2∑f=12​ξ2Xi,f(β),(σf(β))2≡1Nsample​L2​(2​ξ2)−1​∑sample∑i=1L2∑f=12​ξ2(Xi,f(β)−μf(β))2.\mu_{f}^{(\beta)}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sample}}L^{2}\left(2\xi^{2}\right)}\sum_{\text{sample}}\sum_{i=1}^{L^{2}}\sum_{f=1}^{2\xi^{2}}X_{i,f}^{(\beta)},\qquad\left(\sigma_{f}^{(\beta)}\right)^{2}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{sample}}L^{2}\left(2\xi^{2}\right)-1}\sum_{\text{sample}}\sum_{i=1}^{L^{2}}\sum_{f=1}^{2\xi^{2}}\left(X_{i,f}^{(\beta)}-\mu_{f}^{(\beta)}\right)^{2}. (220)

Eq. 220 replaces Eq. 12 for computing μf(β)\mu_{f}^{(\beta)} and σf(β)\sigma_{f}^{(\beta)} in the four-band model. We then use these values to standardize XinitX_{\mathrm{init}} and XtgtX_{\mathrm{tgt}} following Eq. 13.

C.2.3 Weight Initialization

The initial values for all NN parameters were drawn from the default distributions in PyTorch’s initialization scheme. Specifically, we use Kaiming (He) [47] initialization for all weight matrices and bias vectors in the input and output layers (i.e. Win,binW_{\text{in}},b_{\text{in}} and Wout,boutW_{\text{out}},b_{\text{out}}) as well as in the FFNs (see Eq. 45) and the MLPs for fθf_{\theta} (from Eq. 219), and in the self-attention mechanism (i.e. WQ(h),WK(h),WV(h),WOW_{Q}^{(h)},W_{K}^{(h)},W_{V}^{(h)},W_{O}). Unlike the general case in Eq. 38, we do not use a learnable bias vector bOb_{O} when mixing information across attention heads. For the LayerNorm operation (see Eq. 42), the weights γ\gamma and the biases β\beta are initialized to all 11’s and all 00’s, respectively. Finally, we choose the learnable scalar ss in Eq. 32 in each attention head to be initialized to 11. All learnable parameters are trained by backpropagation to minimize the loss.

C.2.4 Results

We train a self-attention model on 10,000 (input,label) 1-RDM pairs at L=6L=6 and L=8L=8, and evaluate on 1,000 held-out systems with L∈{10,12,…,50}L\in\{10,12,\ldots,50\}. For each test instance we run two HF solvers with identical tolerance and settings: (i) initialized from a random 1-RDM, and (ii) initialized from the NN-predicted final 1-RDM. We report the percent reduction in iteration count. At L=50L=50 the mean reduction is 91.63%91.63\%. Results for all LL are in Fig. 12 and Tab. 4.

In order to test how well the NN generalizes to larger system sizes, we also computed the MSE loss between the predicted final 1-RDM from the NN and the true final 1-RDM for up to L=50L=50, where the MSE is defined as in Eq. 23. The results can be seen in Fig. 13.

Appendix D Square-lattice Hubbard model

At temperature T=0T=0 and for collinear states OσO_{\sigma} is a projector onto the occupied subspace,

We set the spin U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry not spontaneously broken, i.e., [O]↑⁣↓=[O]↓⁣↑=0[O]_{\uparrow\downarrow}=[O]_{\downarrow\uparrow}=0. We further assume spin fillings to be

Nocc,↑=Nocc,↓,N_{\mathrm{occ},\uparrow}=N_{\mathrm{occ},\downarrow}, (232)

but we do not impose translational symmetry. For the on-site Hubbard interaction, it may generate a mixing between 𝒌\bm{k} and 𝒌+𝑸,\bm{k}+\bm{Q}, if translational symmetry spontaneously breaks. At each iteration we diagonalize and refill the Nocc,σN_{\mathrm{occ},\sigma} lowest eigenstates to update 1-RDM. This HF set-up provides true final 1-RDM labels (benchmarks to train and validate the ML model), and to quantify HF iteration savings at fixed discretization, filling, and UU.

D.2 ML Results

Despite spontaneous translation breaking, the order parameters of Hubbard model can be simplified to be similar enough to the translation-invariant case to use the same techniques according to Sec. A.1.1.

Label the L×LL\times L BZ grid by integer coordinates Eq. 48.

We investigated two approaches. Firstly, we trained a self-attention NN on the combined L2L^{2}-long sequence. Additionally, for this model we also trained SIRENs separately on the central diagonal and off-diagonal elements, and then combined the outputs to form the new 1-RDM. For both models, the training data was generated via HF calculations (for systems with small LL) that had a convergence criterion of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}. The trained model was then used to predict a density matrix for larger LL which was subsequently used as the initial guess for the density matrix in the HF algorithm, using the same convergence criterion.

The self-attention NN was trained only for U=1U=1 (due to limited data), while we also trained additional SIREN models for U=2U=2 and U=3U=3. In each case, the resultant reduction in the number of HF iterations required for convergence was noted, where the reduction is defined as the percent difference between the average number of HF iterations before and after using the NN outputs as the initial guess for the density matrix.

The training process for both NN architectures is detailed below.

D.2.1 Self-Attention NN

For each 𝒌\bm{k} we transform 1-RDM into a real vector of length 2​ξ22\xi^{2} and standardize them as described in Sec. A.1.2 and Sec. A.1.1.

For the self-attention NN for the Hubbard model, we initialize WinW_{\text{in}} and WoutW_{\text{out}} from a truncated normal distribution with σ=0.02\sigma=0.02. Kaiming (He) normal initialization [47] is used for the learnable weight matrices in the feedforward layers, while Xavier (Glorot) initialization [38] is used for each of the matrices WQ(h)W_{Q}^{(h)}, WK(h)W_{K}^{(h)}, WV(h)W_{V}^{(h)}, WOW_{O} in the attention heads. The matrix of frequencies WrW_{r} from Eq. 25 is initialized with values drawn from a standard normal distribution. Furthermore, the weights γ\gamma for the LayerNorm operation from Eq. 42, the vector of coefficients CC (Eq. 28), the power pp (Eq. 29), and the learnable scalar ss (Eq. 32) are each initialized to be 11. All bias vectors are set to 00 initially. After initialization, these learnable parameters are updated by backpropagation to minimize the loss, as indicated in Sec. A.1.3.

In order to train the NN, we used a custom learning rate schedule consisting of a linear warmup phase followed by cosine annealing (without restarts) [78], which is a well-established method for training self-attention models with adaptive optimizers. This learning rate cycle is repeated twice: initially, we train for 500500 epochs, and then for 50005000 epochs. Each time, the warmup phase lasts for 2020 epochs followed by cosine decay for the rest of the cycle. Thus, we train for a total of 55005500 training epochs. Nevertheless, we found that the loss decreased to a minimum around 32003200 epochs, which is the checkpoint used for evaluation. The self-attention NN was trained on 467467 samples (i.e. input/output pairs) for L=8L=8 and 10011001 samples for L=10L=10, and performance was observed to vary noticeably based on the random seed used (where “random seed” refers to the initializer for the pseudorandom number generator(s) of the computer), corroborating the findings in [144]. A full list of hyperparameters can be seen in Tab. 5.

D.2.2 SIREN

As aforementioned, each set of “significant” points forms a tensor of shape L×L×2×2L\times L\times 2\times 2. To take full advantage of dimensionality reduction, we trained a separate SIREN for every index of the 2×22\times 2 matrix at each 𝒌\bm{k} that had significantly nonzero elements. That is, each SIREN was trained on an L×LL\times L matrix (for the Hubbard model, each of the SIRENs was trained on L=8L=8 ), and the outputs were then combined to reconstruct the original shape. Of course, just like with the Richardson model, we extend the size of the matrix to (L+1)×(L+1)(L+1)\times(L+1) by “wrapping” around the first element of each dimension in order to satisfy normalization constraints, as described in Sec. A.2.2. Due to the large search space of possible hyperparameter configurations, we again used TPE [6] through the Optuna and RayTune libraries to optimize hyperparameters individually for each SIREN model trained in this way.

D.2.3 Results

After training, we evaluate acceleration by re-running HF initialized with the NN-predicted final 1-RDM and reporting the percent reduction in iteration count relative to HF started from a random 1-RDM under the same tolerance and settings. Results are shown in Tab. 6.
